issues.title: 20 Weeks Strong, and the Valley Opener is Saturday
issues.blurb: Morgan the 12-year-old chukar dog, grilled quail for the new season, the case for a gun sling, and the valley duck opener is six days out.
issues.body:
## Sunday, October 18, 2026

Welcome back, and thank you. This is the 20th consecutive week we have landed in your inbox, and to everyone who has been with us since the beginning, it means more than we can say. You will get everything you have come to expect today, and the new additions we previewed in Issue #018 (the marketplace, refuge-level weather, and the app) are still coming together behind the scenes, with more to share soon. The calendar is loaded: the X zones close today, quail and chukar opened yesterday, and the Balance of State duck opener is Saturday. This week we are grilling the first quail of the season, making the case for the gun sling you will wish you had bought, clearing a flood pipe with Tad A. before the water goes on, meeting Morgan, a 12-year-old bird dog who has not slowed down one bit, and handing the mic back to Weston W. for a turkey story where his dad was very nearly the one who got hunted. Let's get into it.

## The Board: Dates and Deadlines

- Today, Sunday, October 18: X zones close. Last light for X-1 through X-7b general deer. General bear in those X zones keeps running through December 27.
- Today, Sunday, October 18: reservation deadline for Wednesday, November 4. Applications for reservation drawings on state-operated areas close 17 days before each hunt, so the deadlines keep rolling: Wednesday, October 21 for Saturday, November 7; Thursday, October 22 for Sunday, November 8; and Sunday, October 25 for Wednesday, November 11. It is $1.34 per hunt choice online, at a license agent, or at a CDFW license sales office. Results post at least seven days before each hunt.
- Quail, chukar, and snipe are open. The all-quail season opened yesterday in Zones Q1 and Q3 and runs to January 31, ten per day. Q2 has been open since September 26. Chukar is open statewide to January 31, six per day. Snipe runs to January 31, eight per day, and needs your free HIP validation. Unless you hunt on a junior license, carry your Upland Game Bird Validation.
- Saturday, October 24: the Balance of State opener. Ducks run to January 31, seven per day, which may include no more than two hen mallards, three pintail, two canvasback, and two redheads. Coots and moorhens are open alongside at 25 per day. Regular-season geese open the same day: 30 per day, up to 20 white and 10 dark, with no more than six white-fronted geese (three in the Sacramento Valley Special Management Area, where white-fronts close after December 21). Have your California Duck Validation, a Federal Duck Stamp signed across the face, and your free HIP validation in hand before the first decoy hits the water.
- Sunday, October 25: B and C zones close. B-1, B-2, B-3, B-5, B-6, C-2, and C-3 general deer all wrap up. Confirm your subzone lines in the 2026 Big Game Digest.
- Sunday, November 1: D zones and archery pheasant. D-3 to D-5, D-6, and D-7 general deer close. The first archery-only pheasant segment also ends November 1 (it reopens December 28 to January 24).
- Saturday, November 7: scaup opens in the Balance of State Zone, two per day, through January 31.
- On the horizon, Saturday, November 14. General pheasant (to December 27; two roosters per day for the first two days, three after that), fall turkey (to December 13, one either sex per day, two per season), and the second dove split (to December 28, 15 per day) all open the same day.
- Bear check. CDFW's posted statewide count is still 226 bears as of September 28, far short of the 1,700 that would close the season early. Licensed hunters can buy two bear tags this license year. Get your tag validated before you transport, and present the skull to CDFW within 10 days for the premolar.
- Report your tags. Filled deer tags must be reported within 30 days of harvest.
- Non-lead, every hunt, no exceptions. Certified non-lead ammunition is required for all firearm hunting in California. On the water, that means non-toxic shot and a shotgun plugged to three shells.

## From Field to Table: Grilled Spatchcocked Quail

Quail and chukar are open everywhere now, and the best thing you can do with the first birds of the year is keep it simple. Splitting a quail flat (spatchcocking) lets it cook evenly and fast over a hot grill, so the skin crisps before the lean breast dries out. Ten minutes on the fire and dinner is done. Chukar work the same way, just a few minutes longer.

You will need: four to six quail or two to three chukar (plucked and skin-on if you can, since the skin protects lean meat), kitchen shears, olive oil, kosher salt, black pepper, three tablespoons of butter melted with two minced garlic cloves, chopped fresh thyme or rosemary, a lemon, and an instant-read thermometer. Optional: a quick brine (a quarter cup of kosher salt dissolved in a quart of cold water), a pinch of red pepper flakes, and a drizzle of honey for the butter.

The method:

1. Clean them up. Pick off any stray feathers and feel for shot. Dig out every pellet you can find and trim any bloodshot meat.
1. Optional brine. Soak the birds in the cold brine in the fridge for about an hour (two at most), then rinse and pat them bone-dry.
1. Spatchcock. Set each bird breast-side down and cut along both sides of the backbone with kitchen shears. Pull the backbone out, flip the bird, and press down on the breastbone until it lies flat.
1. Season. Rub with olive oil and season well with salt and pepper.
1. Grill hot. Over medium-high direct heat, cook skin-side down for three to four minutes, then flip for another two to four minutes. Chukar need a few minutes more per side.
1. Baste and rest. Brush on the garlic herb butter in the last minute, pull the birds, and rest them three minutes. Finish with a squeeze of lemon and eat them with your hands.

Doneness and safety note: USDA guidance is 165 degrees for poultry, game birds included. Check the thickest part of the breast near the bone, and keep an eye on it, because small birds blow past done in a hurry. Remind everyone at the table to chew carefully in case you missed a pellet. Wear nitrile gloves when you clean birds, and with afternoons still warm this month, get your birds out of the vest and into the cooler from Issue #15 quickly (the cool-fast rule from Issue #7 applies to birds, too).

## Gear Check: The Gun Sling

![](/media/e3953083-19f8-45c6-8b08-2372c7ac1f91.png)

Whether you are chasing ducks or still after deer, don't get caught deep in the backwoods or out in the flooded ground with both hands full, wishing you had a sling.

Our value pick is a padded neoprene sling with swivels. The stretchy padding soaks up bounce so the gun rides lighter, and a non-slip backing keeps it on your shoulder. Get one long enough to fit over waders and a heavy coat. Expect roughly $25 to $45, so check current pricing. Floor option: a basic nylon sling for around $10. Step up: premium slings with better hardware run several times the price.

Before you buy: make sure your gun has sling swivel studs (plenty of duck guns don't). And always unload before you cross a ditch, climb a fence, or step into the boat. Pair it with your shooting sticks from Issue #11 or the waders from Issue #16.

## The Showcase

![](/media/18b204ba-092f-466e-8835-8c3aefcd8f58.png)

This week's Showcase is the unglamorous side of duck season, and we love it. Tad A. of Durham sent in a photo of a flood pipe halfway choked with mud, and he spent part of his week digging it out so the water can go on before the opener. Every great morning in the blind starts with work nobody sees: pipes, boards, levees, and blinds. If you have not walked your drains and inlets yet, take this as your reminder. Nice work, Tad.

The Showcase is exclusive to subscribers, so the folks on this list see it first. Next week it could be yours: the first greenhead of the valley season, a covey flush, a last-weekend B-zone buck, or the work that got your spot ready. Hit reply with your photo or clip and a sentence about it, and tell us how you want to be credited (we run first name, last initial, and town). The best one each week runs up top and earns a permanent spot on our subscribers-only Showcase page.

## Dog of the Week

![](/media/d893329f-64a8-4195-94cd-ebd430bf9e36.jpg)

Meet "Morgan" (Owner: Allen C., Forest Ranch)

Morgan is 12 years old and still locking up on birds like it is the first season. Allen sent us a shot of Morgan on point on a chukar at Clear Creek Sports Club near Corning, and the intensity in that pose is something a lot of young dogs are still working toward. Here is to the gray-muzzled veterans who keep showing up and doing the job.

Want your dog featured? Hit reply, send us a clean photo of your hunting partner, and give us a quick 2 to 3 sentence blurb on what they hunt and where they earn their kibble. Pointers, flushers, retrievers, and the occasional very good mutt all qualify. Missed a week? Catch up on every dog we have featured on our Dog of the Week page.

## From the Field: Almost Spurred by Thanksgiving Dinner

"This thing was running full speed from 100 yards away, right at us."

Weston W. was 15, hunting turkeys with his dad in an almond orchard in Durham, right along Butte Creek. Shortly after sunup, a big flock of toms and hens came working across the orchard about 100 yards out. All they had was a box call, a hen decoy, and a jake decoy, and no time to set up properly. His dad got the hen out, they each grabbed a tree, and the jake never made it out of his dad's hand.

The flock was not paying them any attention. So his dad started bobbing the jake up and down, trying to get something to notice. Then one tom broke from the group, and he was not coming for the hen.

Submitted by Weston W., Durham

Read the full story on norcalhunt.com/fieldstories.

Got a hunt that turned into a story? A first bird, a near miss, a morning that went sideways and turned out better for it? Hit reply and tell it the way you would at the tailgate, and we will clean it up. Catch up on the ones we have already run on our field stories page.

## Community: Help Us Build the Pack

This briefing gets sharper when we hear from you. Drop us a quick reply and tell us:

1. What zones are you hunting right now?
1. Where are you spending opening weekend: the duck blind, the quail hills, or one last deer hunt?
1. What would make the weekly briefing more useful to you?

Last week's poll: what did you shoot your first buck with? The answers came in spread evenly across the board, but the .30-06 took the lead by a hair. A classic for a reason.

This week's poll: what is the longest distance you have ever killed an animal at?

### What is the longest distance you have ever killed an animal at?

Got a hunting partner in the foothills, the rice, or along the riverbanks? Forward this briefing and point them to norcalhunt.com. Twenty weeks in, word of mouth from real hunters is still how we grow.

## Local Services: Find It Close to Home

Steel shot for Saturday, a new sling, a processor with room for your last buck, or someone to help you get the water on: somebody close to you has it. Our local services page keeps the NorCal businesses that treat hunters right all in one place. Check it out at norcalhunt.com/localboys and if your shop belongs on it, hit reply.

## Conditions: Heat, Then a Hint of Rain

The past week ran hot, with Chico topping out near 91 on Thursday. The National Weather Service has today sunny with a high near 82, then a slight chance of rain Monday as highs drop into the low 70s. On the fire side, the Fork Fire in Shasta County is now fully contained, but CAL FIRE is tracking the newer Blue Fire in Shasta County (38 acres, 60 percent contained) and two small fires in Humboldt County, the Surgone and Marshall fires. Sierra hunters should note the Dome Fire in Mariposa County, about 6,800 acres and 86 percent contained.

Before you load the truck:

- Confirm restrictions for your unit. Forest orders and burn bans change by district. Check fire.ca.gov and your local forest before you go.
- Don't trust one shower. A slight chance of rain will not wet down cured grass and timber. Mind your exhaust, your drag chains, and your campfire plans.
- Check the forecast Friday night. Opener week weather is still taking shape, and wind and cloud cover will make or break Saturday. Look again before you set the alarm.
- Cool your birds fast. Warm afternoons will still sour ducks and quail left in a vest or a bucket. Get them on ice.

Stay safe out there, get your gear cleaned, and we'll see you in the field.

The NorCal Hunt Team

issues.title: The Parking Brake Buck
issues.blurb: Sadie the golden pup, a co-founder's Colorado scouting trip, Quail and chukar open Saturday, the valley duck opener is two weeks out, and a seared venison heart.
issues.body:
## Sunday, October 11, 2026

Welcome back. After last week's lighter preview issue, every section is back this week and loaded with good stuff. October is doing what October does: stacking seasons on top of each other faster than you can clean your gear. Quail and chukar open Saturday in Q1 and Q3, the X zones close next Sunday, and the Balance of State duck opener is now two weeks out with reservation deadlines rolling this week. This issue we're putting the deer heart to work in a hard, fast sear, making the case for the least glamorous piece of gear you own (a shovel, and yes, one of you knows exactly why), and taking you to Colorado with co-founder Weston W. as he scouts for his October bull. Then Weston tells the story of the buck that should have been his first, which involves a 3x3, a tripod, and a side by side with other plans. Let's get into it.

## The Board: Dates and Deadlines

- Today, Sunday, October 11: reservation deadline for Wednesday, October 28. Applications for reservation drawings on state-operated areas close 17 days before each hunt, so the deadlines keep rolling: today for Wednesday the 28th, Wednesday, October 14 for Saturday the 31st, and Thursday, October 15 for Sunday, November 1. It's $1.34 per hunt choice online, at a license agent, or at a CDFW license sales office.
- Opener reservation results. Results post at least seven days before each hunt, so if you applied for October 24, check your account by Saturday the 17th.
- Saturday, October 17: quail, chukar, and snipe. All-quail season opens in Zones Q1 and Q3 and runs to January 31, ten quail per day. Q2 has been open since September 26. Chukar opens statewide the same day, six per day, and runs to January 31. Snipe also opens October 17, eight per day, and needs your free HIP validation. In Q1, mountain-quail-only wraps up Friday the 16th.
- Sunday, October 18: X zones close. X-1 through X-7b general deer closes next Sunday. General bear in those X zones opened yesterday, October 10, and runs to December 27.
- Saturday, October 24: the Balance of State opener. Ducks run to January 31, seven per day, which may include no more than two hen mallards, three pintail, two canvasback, and two redheads. Scaup stays closed until November 7 (two per day after that). Regular-season geese open the same day: 30 per day, up to 20 white and 10 dark, with no more than six white-fronted geese (three in the Sacramento Valley Special Management Area through December 21). Have your California Duck Validation, a Federal Duck Stamp signed across the face, and your free HIP validation in hand before the first decoy hits the water.
- Sunday, October 25: B and C zones close. B-1, B-2, B-3, B-5, B-6, C-2, and C-3 general deer all wrap up. D-3 to D-5, D-6, and D-7 run through November 1. Confirm your subzone lines in the 2026 Big Game Digest.
- Bear check. CDFW's statewide count stood at 226 bears as of September 28, far short of the 1,700 that would close the season early. Tag validation and premolar submission are still mandatory.
- On the horizon, Saturday, November 14. Pheasant (to December 27), fall turkey (to December 13, one per day, two per season), and dove's second split (to December 28) all open the same day. Archery-only pheasant has been open since October 10.
- Report your tags. Filled deer tags must be reported within 30 days of harvest.
- Non-lead, every hunt, no exceptions. Certified non-lead ammunition is required for all firearm hunting in California. On the water, that means non-toxic shot and a shotgun plugged to three shells.

## From Field to Table: Seared Venison Heart

Back in Issue #6 we told you to save the heart, and in Issue #14 we walked you through pulling the pluck. Here's why. A deer heart is a dense, fine-grained, hard-working muscle that eats more like a lean steak than anything people picture when they hear "organ meat." Sliced and seared hot, it's one of the best bites on the animal, and it's ready in about ten minutes.

You will need: one deer heart, coarse salt and black pepper, a high-heat oil or tallow, two tablespoons of butter, two crushed garlic cloves, a sprig of thyme or rosemary, and a cast-iron skillet. Optional: sliced onions to cook in the drippings, flaky salt, or a spoon of chimichurri to finish.

The method:

1. Clean it up. Trim off the fat cap and cut away the top of the heart where the valves and arteries attach. Split it open, rinse out any clotted blood, and trim the tough inner membranes and connective tissue. What's left is clean, dark-red muscle.
1. Slice it. Cut into steaks or strips about a half inch thick. Pat them bone-dry.
1. Optional soak. If yours was bloody, soak the slices in salted water in the fridge for a few hours, then dry them again.
1. Season and sear. Salt and pepper well. Get the cast iron smoking hot with a film of oil and sear one to two minutes per side. Don't crowd the pan.
1. Baste. Drop the heat, add butter, garlic, and herbs, and spoon the foaming butter over the slices for 30 seconds.
1. Rest and slice. Rest two to three minutes, slice thin against the grain, and serve it on toast, in tacos, or next to eggs at deer camp.

Doneness and safety note: heart is lean, and the second you overcook it, it turns rubbery. Many hunters pull it at a rosy medium-rare the same way they treat backstrap (Issue #8). USDA's conservative guidance for organ meats and venison is 160 degrees, so if you're cooking for kids, older folks, or anyone pregnant, or you'd simply rather not gamble, cook it through, or braise it low and slow like the tough cuts in Issue #11. Organs spoil faster than muscle, so get the heart into a bag and onto ice in the field, cook it within a couple of days or vacuum seal it (Issue #7), and wear nitrile gloves while you trim.

## Gear Check: The Shovel (Yes, Really)

![](/media/9a079a6b-62ec-42e4-9fd2-e0c93c3611d9.png)

We know. A shovel. Stay with us. One NorCalHunt subscriber, who will remain nameless (you know who you are), recently learned that mud and sand don't care how good your truck is. When you're buried to the axle on a two-track miles from pavement, you're either digging yourself out or waiting at the mercy of whoever drives by next. Better to have it and not need it than need it and not have it.

Our value pick is the GroundWork 49 in. Hardwood Handle Round Point Shovel from Tractor Supply. You get a steel round point head with a lacquer finish to help it hold up to wear, a full-length 49-inch hardwood handle for real leverage when you're digging out a tire, and a nonslip end grip. It runs about $25, so check current pricing. Keep it out of the rain between trips so the wood handle lasts.

Floor option: the old rusty one in your shed, for free. Clean the blade, check the handle for cracks, and throw it in the truck today. Whatever you carry, it rides in the bed next to the cooler from Issue #15 and the meat frame from Issue #12.

When you're stuck: stop spinning the second you stop moving forward. Dig out in front of all four tires, not just behind, clear anything you're high-centered on, and stuff brush or branches under the drive tires before you ease back on the throttle.

## The Showcase

![](/media/556505ec-f8e5-4f1d-9928-d2b21339dc02.png)

This week's Showcase is an inside look at life on the NorCalHunt crew. Co-founder Weston W. of Durham spent last weekend scouting Colorado ahead of his October bull elk hunt, and this is the shot he brought home: the sun going down over a hillside of aspens gone full gold. No antlers in the frame yet, just the kind of evening that makes all the scouting miles worth it. We'll let you know how the bull hunt shakes out.

The Showcase is exclusive to subscribers, so the folks on this list see it first. Next week it could be yours: a buck on the tailgate, a covey flush on opening morning, the first greenhead of the valley season. Hit reply with your photo or clip and a sentence about it, and tell us how you want to be credited (we run first name, last initial, and town). The best one each week runs up top and earns a permanent spot on our subscribers-only Showcase page.

## Dog of the Week

![](/media/3c21f71d-a56d-4aea-8c0e-75fb6729a17e.png)

Meet "Sadie" (Owners: Matt P. and Emma H., Chico)

Sadie is a golden retriever pup out of Chico, and her owners will be the first to tell you she is a passenger princess in the making. She's still a puppy, which means the window seat, the truck rides, and the best spot in the cab are all hers to claim for now. She's the first golden retriever we've featured in Dog of the Week, and she earned the spot.

Want your dog featured? Hit reply, send us a clean photo of your hunting partner, and give us a quick 2 to 3 sentence blurb on what they hunt and where they earn their kibble. Pointers, flushers, retrievers, and the occasional very good mutt all qualify. Missed a week? Catch up on every dog we've featured on our past Dogs of the Week page.

## From the Field: The Parking Brake Buck

"One second, two seconds, three, and my dad said 'take it.'"

Weston was 13, hunting B zone with his dad on private ground west of Redding. It was October, and they'd spent the whole day on the side by side: some does, no legal bucks, and daylight running out. So they swung back to a spot they'd already checked twice, an opening ringed in thick brush that you couldn't see into until you crested the hill.

They rolled over the top slow, and there he was: a 3x3 standing broadside in the opening. His dad called it a shooter, set the parking brake, and put up the sticks. Weston settled the crosshairs and took his time on the first buck of his life. Maybe a little too much time. Somewhere around seven seconds, he felt his dad bump him in the back.

What was happening behind him, and why he wouldn't trade it for the buck, is the part you'll want to read.

Submitted by Weston W.

Read the full story on norcalhunt.com/fieldstories.

Got a hunt that turned into a story? A first buck, a near miss, a day that went sideways and turned out better for it? Hit reply and tell it the way you would at the tailgate, and we'll clean it up. Catch up on the ones we've already run on our field stories page.

## Community: Help Us Build the Pack

This briefing gets sharper when we hear from you. Drop us a quick reply and tell us:

1. What zones are you hunting right now?
1. What's next on your calendar: quail, chukar, ducks, or a late deer tag?
1. What would make the weekly briefing more useful to you?

This week's poll: everybody remembers their first buck, and the gun or bow that took it. What did you shoot your first buck with?

### What did you shoot your first buck with?

Got a hunting partner in the foothills, the rice, or along the riverbanks? Forward this briefing and point them to norcalhunt.com. Word of mouth from real hunters is how we grow.

## Local Services: Find It Close to Home

Quail vests, steel shot for the opener, a processor with room for your last buck, or a tow when the shovel isn't enough: somebody close to you has it. Our local services page keeps the NorCal businesses that treat hunters right all in one place. Check it out, and if your shop belongs on it, hit reply. norcalhunt.com/localboys

## Conditions: A Dry Week, and Fire Season Isn't Over

No rain in the valley forecast this week. The National Weather Service has the Chico area sunny all week, with highs in the 70s early on warming into the mid-80s by Thursday and Friday, lows from the mid-40s to mid-50s, and northwest gusts near 30 mph on Sunday. Close to home, CAL FIRE lists the Fork Fire in Shasta County at 59 acres and 75 percent contained. Sierra hunters should note the Dome Fire in Mariposa County, now about 6,800 acres and 61 percent contained, and the newer Piute Fire in Tuolumne County, small but only 5 percent contained. Before you load the truck:

- Confirm restrictions for your unit. Forest orders and burn bans change by district. Check fire.ca.gov and your local forest before you go.
- Respect the wind. On gusty north wind days, skip the long push into dry grass and timber.
- Don't be the spark. A hot exhaust parked in dry grass is all it takes. Mind your side by side, your drag chains, and your campfire plans where bans are in place. And set that parking brake.
- Cool it fast. Mornings are cool, but mid-80s afternoons will still sour meat. Get your buck (and that heart) on ice quickly.

Stay safe out there, get your gear cleaned, and we'll see you in the field.

The NorCal Hunt Team

## Sunday, October 4, 2026

Happy Sunday, and welcome back. This week's briefing runs a little lighter than usual, and that is on purpose: we are not skipping a week, we are building. Behind the scenes, the team is putting together a bigger, sharper norcalhunt.com, built to give you exactly what you need for the rest of this season and every season you choose to spend with us. This issue is your first look. You still get every date that matters, and October has plenty: Northeastern Zone ducks opened yesterday, the X zones came online, and the valley duck opener is under three weeks out with a reservation deadline this Wednesday. Let's get into it.

## The Board: Dates and Deadlines

Today, Sunday October 4: C-1 and C-4 general deer close. Last light on those two. C-2 and C-3 keep running through October 25.

Through Monday, October 5: Balance of State early goose. The short early season (October 3 to 5) is for large Canada geese only. Two more mornings if you have a field lined up.

Northeastern Zone waterfowl is open. Ducks opened Saturday and run to January 13, seven per day, which may include no more than two hen mallards, three pintail, two canvasback, two redheads, and two scaup. Canada geese opened the same day and run to January 10, with white and white-fronted geese running October 3 to November 29 and again January 1 to 13.

The X zones are in. X-1 through X-7b general deer opened Saturday and runs to October 18, draw tags only. General bear in those X zones opens Saturday, October 10.

Wednesday, October 7: reservation deadline for the valley opener. Applications for reservation drawings on state-operated areas close 17 days before each hunt, so Wednesday is your last day to apply for the October 24 opener. It costs $1.34 per hunt choice online, at a license agent, or at a CDFW license sales office, and results post at least seven days before the hunt.

Deer season is wide open. Most B zones run through October 25, but a few subzones close earlier, so confirm yours. D3 to D5 runs through November 1 on the D3-5 tag, and D6 and D7 also run through November 1. Check your subzone lines in the 2026 Big Game Digest before you climb an unfamiliar ridge.

Saturday, October 17: quail and chukar. The all-quail season opens in Zones Q1 and Q3, and chukar opens statewide the same day. Q2 has been open since September 26. Ten quail per day in aggregate.

Saturday, October 24: the Balance of State opener. Ducks and regular-season geese run to January 31. Scaup stays closed until November 7. Your California Duck Validation, a signed Federal Duck Stamp (ink across the face), and your free HIP validation all need to be in hand before you set a single decoy.

On the horizon. Pheasant and fall turkey both open Saturday, November 14.

Report your tags. Filled deer tags must be reported within 30 days of harvest. Do it from the truck while the details are fresh.

Non-lead, every hunt, no exceptions. Certified non-lead ammunition is required for all firearm hunting in California. On the water that means non-toxic shot and a shotgun plugged to three shells.

## The Next Chapter: What We Are Building

Every reply you have sent us since day one has been read, and a lot of them have shaped what comes next. You told us what you check before a hunt, what you wish you could find in one place, and what keeps you coming back on Sunday. We are grateful for every word of it, and we are using that feedback to rebuild the website around your needs and preferences.

Here is a first look at a few of the things on the way:

A marketplace built for NorCal hunters. A place to find the gear, services, and local businesses that serve this community, without wading through the noise of a national site. More details soon, and if you run a shop or service that belongs there, hit reply and get on our list early.

Weather built for where you actually hunt. A few weeks back, in Issue #016, we asked what makes a duck day for you, and the options were wind, clouds and rain, migration, and hunter reports. That question was not random. We are building a unique weather indexing tool for refuges and hunt areas, so instead of a city forecast that tells you nothing about the marsh, you get conditions tied to the ground you are hunting.

NorCalHunt in your pocket. We are also building a NorCalHunt app, so the dates, deadlines, and conditions you count on every Sunday ride along in the truck, the blind, and deer camp. It is still in the works, and we will share more as it comes together.

Put together, it adds up to a more robust NorCalHunt: more depth, more tools, and more of what you need right when you need it, whether you are planning a hunt on Tuesday night or checking conditions from the tailgate before shoot time. We are not just adding features. We are building a service that works as hard as you do from opener to closer.

The weekly briefing is not going anywhere, and neither is anything else you count on. The Showcase, Dog of the Week, field stories, and every other feature you know will keep growing right alongside the rest of NorCalHunt.

## Your Season, Your Stories

We know most of you are in the thick of deer season right now, and the ducks are about to stack on top of it. We cannot wait to hear how it goes. Send us the buck on the tailgate, the first greenhead of the year, the sunrise you almost did not get up for, and the story of the morning that went sideways and turned out better for it. The hunts you are on this fall are the ones your kids and grandkids will be hearing about at the tailgate someday, and we would be honored to help tell them.

issues.body:
## Sunday, September 27, 2026

Welcome back. The calendar flipped hard this weekend. Valley quail opened yesterday in Zone Q2, the D-3 to D-5 deer zones came online the same morning, and next Saturday brings the first water of the year: the Northeastern Zone duck opener and a three-day early goose hunt in the valley. You also told us exactly what gets you out of bed for ducks (clouds and rain, no contest), and the state just declared an emergency over a winter that may deliver plenty of both. So this issue leans into the wet season ahead: a grilled quail recipe for the birds in your vest, a blind bag that keeps your gear organized and off the wet floor, and the dates you cannot miss. Let's get into it.

## The Board: Dates and Deadlines

Today, Sunday September 27: B-4 general deer closes. Last day on B-4's early calendar (August 22 to September 27). The rest of B-zone (B-1, B-2, B-3, B-5) stays open through October 25, and B-6 runs to October 18.

Opened yesterday: D-3, D-4, and D-5 general deer. September 26 to November 1, one forked-horn buck or better per tag, and a D3-5 tag is good in all three zones. D-6 and D-7 have been open since September 19. If you hunt D-7, CWD sampling is mandatory within 10 days of harvest.

Opened yesterday: valley quail in Zone Q2. The all-quail season runs through January 31 with a daily bag of 10 in any combination and triple that in possession. Zone Q1 is open right now for mountain quail only (since September 12), and both Q1 and Q3 open for all quail October 17, along with chukar statewide. You need an Upland Game Bird Validation unless you hunt on a junior license.

Saturday, October 3: first water of the year. The Northeastern Zone duck season opens and runs to January 13. The same morning, Balance of State gets its early large Canada goose hunt, October 3 to 5, large Canadas only (closed in the North Coast Special Management Area). X-1 through X-7b drawn deer hunts also open October 3.

Saturday, October 24: Balance of State ducks, four weeks out. Seven ducks a day, no more than 2 hen mallards, 3 pintail, 2 canvasback, 2 redhead, and 2 scaup once scaup opens November 7. New this year: the speck (white-fronted goose) limit drops to 6 a day, and only 3 inside the Sacramento Valley Special Management Area. Get your Duck Validation, a Federal Duck Stamp signed across the face, and your free HIP validation squared away now.

Tagged a buck? Report it. Successful deer hunters must report within 30 days of harvest or by January 31, whichever comes first. Unsuccessful hunters report by January 31. Bear tags get reported immediately after take.

Non-lead, every hunt. Certified non-lead ammunition is required for all firearm hunting in California. On the water that means non-toxic shot and a shotgun plugged to three shells.

## From Field to Table: Grilled Spatchcocked Quail

Quail are small, lean, and unforgiving of a long cook, which is exactly why this method works. Flatten the bird, brine it briefly, and put it over high heat for a few minutes a side. You get crisp skin, juicy meat, and dinner on the table about ten minutes after the grill is hot.

You will need: four quail, plucked with the skin on (plan two per person), kitchen shears, a brine of 4 cups cold water with 1/4 cup kosher salt and 2 tablespoons brown sugar or honey, olive oil or melted butter, black pepper, a lemon, a couple of cloves of garlic, fresh thyme or rosemary, and an instant-read thermometer.

The method:

1. Pluck, don't skin. Quail skin is the only fat these birds bring, and it protects the meat on the grill. Feathers come out easiest while the birds are still warm. Pick out every pellet and trim any shot-damaged meat.
1. Spatchcock. Set the bird breast down, cut along both sides of the backbone with shears, and lift the backbone out. Flip it and press flat with the heel of your hand until you hear the breastbone give.
1. Brine short. One to two hours in the fridge, no longer. Small birds turn salty fast. Rinse and pat completely dry, because dry skin is crisp skin.
1. Season. Rub with oil or butter, pepper, grated garlic, lemon zest, and chopped herbs.
1. Cook hot and fast. Over a hot grill, skin side down, 3 to 4 minutes until the skin crisps and releases, then flip for 2 to 3 minutes. No grill? A ripping-hot skillet works the same way with a second pan set on top to keep the birds flat.
1. Rest and finish. Three minutes on the board, a squeeze of lemon, and serve with your fingers.

Doneness and safety note: unlike the duck breast in Issue #16 that we serve rosy, treat quail like any other game bird and cook it to 165 degrees in the thickest part of the breast. The brine keeps it juicy even fully done. Wear nitrile gloves when you clean birds, and do not let a vest full of quail ride around in a warm afternoon: get them cool fast (Issue #7) and into the cooler from Issue #15 before the drive home.

## Gear Check: A Blind Bag That Earns Its Spot

![](/media/9e6b6b28-2ed2-43aa-91e5-90227e1066ba.png)

The Northeastern opener is Saturday, and the valley follows in four weeks. Before you head out, get the loose shell boxes, the call lanyard, the phone, and the sunglasses out of your jacket pockets and into one bag that keeps it all organized and off the wet blind floor.

Our pick is the Drake Waterfowl Large Blind Bag. It looks too small at first glance (about 18 by 11 by 10 inches and 3.6 pounds), but it swallows a full hunt's worth of gear. The main compartment and internal pockets have room for your calls, spare shells, gloves, a thermos, snacks, and a headlamp, while the outside handles the stuff you reach for most. Two external side pouches each hold a box of shells, a strap system on the lid carries a jacket, and a hard-sided external sunglasses case means no more scratched lenses by 9 a.m. The phone sleeve keeps water off your screen and still lets you use the touchscreen. The bottom is TPU, so it shrugs off a muddy pit floor or a wet boat deck, and it tucks into a corner of the blind without taking over. It runs around $85, so check current pricing.

The honest trade-off: this is an organizer with a tough, water-resistant bottom, not a submersible dry bag. If it goes over the side of the boat, fish it out fast. Pair it with the waders from Issue #16 and you are set for the opener.

This black Lab just earned her AKC Senior Hunter title, and she did it in style. Marv and the M. O. ## Conditions: Fire Season Winding Down, a Wet Winter Lining Up

The Lucas Fire is out. Crews reached full containment on September 20 at 4,128 acres, and every remaining evacuation order has been lifted. If your blacktail plans run into the Hunter Point area of the Mendocino National Forest, confirm with the forest before you go, since suppression repair work there kept some roads and trails closed.

Fire season is not over. This past week's heat pushed temperatures into the 90s with humidity in the 20s before a cooler, more seasonable pattern moved in. The grass is still cured, and any north wind event can bring back red flag conditions with a day's notice. Mind your exhaust and drag chains, keep the truck off dry grass, and check fire.ca.gov and your local forest before you head out.

El Niño is coming, and it looks big. The state declared an emergency on September 21 to get ahead of flooding, and federal forecasters now give better than 90 percent odds of a very strong El Niño this fall and winter. The wetter-than-normal signal is strongest for Southern California early on and spreads across the state by midwinter, so NorCal is not guaranteed a soaker. But if it delivers, that is flooded fields, low skies, and exactly the duck weather you just voted for.

Plan for wet access. A big rain year means muddy levee roads, rising creeks, and flooded low-water crossings. Pack a shovel and traction boards in the truck, and never drive into moving water.

Stay safe out there, get your gear cleaned, and we'll see you in the field.

The NorCal Hunt Team

issues.blurb: A NorCal guide on getting women into waterfowl, plus the opener countdown, the waders to buy now, and Hooey in Dog of the Week.
issues.body:
## Sunday, September 20, 2026

Welcome back. Deer season is in the heat of it, with B, C, and D zones open or opening soon, and the duck opener is now about five weeks out on top of it. The big one this week is in From the Field: Laura Allen of MOA Outfitters wrote in about building a guide service to welcome women into the blind, and it is exactly the kind of submission we love to run. Around it we have a quick refresher on breasting out a duck before opening morning, the value waders to buy now before the shelves empty, a goose hunt from MOA in the Showcase, Hooey in Dog of the Week, and the paperwork you cannot skip. One favor: take this week's poll in the community section, we want to know what makes the ideal duck day. If you are hunting A-zone, today is your last light, so make it count. Everybody else, the season is wide open. Let's get into it.

## The Board: Dates and Deadlines

Today, Sunday September 20: A-zone general closes. This is the last day of the state's longest general season (August 8 to September 20), one buck per tag. Hunt water, feed, and shade at first and last light, and if you fill it, the next section is for you.

B-zone general is running. B1, B2, B3, B5, and B6 are open rifle September 19 to October 25, one buck per tag. B-4 runs its own earlier calendar (August 22 to September 27), so those zones close next Sunday. Confirm your exact subzone lines in the 2026 Big Game Digest before you climb an unfamiliar ridge.

Deer country keeps opening. The C zones came in September 19, and the D zones come online through late September and October, dates varying by subzone. If the foothills or the Sierra are on your calendar, check your subzone opener now, not the night before.

General bear rides with your deer tag. It runs concurrent with your general deer season into late December, or closes early if the statewide take hits 1,700 bears. It is non-lead, no bait, no dogs, with tag validation, premolar submission, and reporting all mandatory. A bear tag in your pocket is a second animal on the same hunt.

Ducks are five weeks out. Do the paperwork now. The Balance of State duck opener lands Saturday, October 24, and runs to January 31, 2027, with a seven-duck daily limit and species sub-limits (including no more than two hen mallards, and caps on pintail, canvasback, redhead, and scaup). The Northeastern Zone opens earlier, October 3. This is the week to pull your California Duck Validation (about $40), your Federal Duck Stamp (sign it across the face in ink or it is not valid), and your free HIP validation, and to confirm the final regs and shoot-time tables at wildlife.ca.gov.

Valley quail opens Saturday, September 26. The all-quail season comes in next Saturday in Zone Q2, which covers most of NorCal. Zones Q1 and Q3 follow on October 17. Check the current Upland Game Bird digest for your zone lines and limits before opening morning.

Non-lead, every hunt, no exceptions. Certified non-lead ammunition is required for all firearm hunting anywhere in California. For ducks that means non-toxic shot (steel and the like), your shotgun plugged to three total shells, and your HIP validation squared away before opener.

## From Field to Table: Breasting Out a Duck, a Quick Refresher Before the Opener

Plenty of you have done this a thousand times, so consider this one for the newer hands and a reminder for the rest of us before the water comes on. The fastest way to clean a duck is to breast it out, and it is about a one-minute job once you have the motion down.

You will need: a sharp knife (the replaceable-blade knife from Issue #4 shines here), nitrile gloves, a bucket or contractor bag for feathers and carcasses, and a cooler on ice (Issue #15) to get birds cold fast.

The method:

1. Lay the bird on its back. Pinch the breast skin at the keel, tear it open, and peel the skin and feathers back off both breast halves.
1. Run your knife down one side of the breastbone, following the bone, and pop each fillet off the ribcage. Two fillets per bird.
1. Trim shot, feathers, and any bloodshot meat. Rinse, pat dry, and onto ice.

That is your move for grilled or seared breasts, poppers, jerky, or the freezer. Fast, clean, no plucking.

Doneness and safety note: duck breast is dark meat and eats best hot and fast with a rosy, medium center, the same principle behind the backstrap in Issue #8, not the fully-done rule we use for ground game. If you would rather not gamble, take it to a fully done 165 degrees. Either way, wear nitrile gloves when you clean birds, keep raw meat cold (the cool-fast rule from Issue #7), and pick out every pellet before it hits the pan or someone's tooth finds it.

## Gear Check: The Waders That Get You Through the Opener

![](/media/c0a5383e-ecc5-46cd-bd94-43d07bcc7a0b.png)

The single most important waterfowl purchase, and the one that sells out first once the water comes on, is a solid pair of chest waders. Buy them now, not the week before the opener when the shelves are picked over.

Our value pick is the TideWe Neoprene Chest Waders. The 3.5mm neoprene keeps you warm in cold water, the insulated rubber boots (600 gram Thinsulate) handle a frosty valley morning, and the seams are stitched, glued, and taped, the same three-step construction the premium brands use. Field reviewers this fall keep landing on them as the best value in the category. They list around $119 and often street closer to $90 to $110, so check current pricing.

## The Showcase

![](/media/7e9feaf6-9cd8-4fc3-a4f6-9be025d30fa3.png)

This week's feature comes straight from MOA Outfitters: a pile of speckled bellies and snow geese from a successful goose hunt in the valley, the kind of morning that has the whole list counting down to the opener. It pairs perfectly with Laura's story further down, a firsthand look at what these hunts are all about. Fine shooting, and thanks for sending it in.

The Showcase is exclusive to subscribers, so the folks on this list see it first. Next week it could be yours, with deer photos rolling in from every open zone and the first of the dog work starting up on the water. A B-zone buck, a first deer, a pile of birds, the retriever on a training bumper, a decoy spread at sunrise. Hit reply with your photo or clip and a sentence about it, and tell us how you want to be credited (we run first name, last initial, and town). The best one each week runs up top and earns a permanent spot on our subscribers-only Showcase page.

## Dog of the Week

![](/media/5b9a0fb0-1c82-4e06-b90d-9e8a02c5022d.jpg)

Meet "Hooey" (Owners: Chad and Allison Porter, Durham)

Hooey is a Durham dog through and through, and his favorite running mate is Bent, our Dog of the Week from Issue #4. The two of them are a team in the blind, happiest retrieving ducks on a cold valley morning. When the season closes, they take it easy, spending their days lounging by the pool and getting out for regular walks with mom and dad, until the next opener.

Pointers, flushers, retrievers, and the occasional very good mutt all qualify. Missed a week? Catch up on every dog we have featured on our Dogs of the Week page.

## From the Field: Building the Next Generation in the Blind

"The idea of meeting strangers on the side of the road out in the middle of nowhere at 4:00 am is a lot less intimidating when you know you are meeting up with a group of like minded women."

With the opener a few weeks out, this week's field note comes from a guide building the next generation of duck hunters in our own backyard. Laura Allen of MOA Outfitters runs a Sacramento Valley guide service dedicated to welcoming women into waterfowl, and she wrote in on why she built it, what it takes to step into a male-driven field, and why she believes the sport's future runs on community over competition. It is worth reading to the last line, and if it sounds like your kind of hunt, you can find MOA Outfitters on our Local Boys page.

## Conditions: Fire Season Is Not Over Yet

issues.blurb: Ground venison spaghetti, the value cooler that saves your September buck, Gus the duck dog, and ducks on the horizon.
issues.body:
## Sunday, September 13, 2026

This is the weekend the calendar starts trading seasons on you. Dove's first split closes Tuesday, so you have two mornings left on the birds. Next weekend does the heavy lifting: B-zone general opens Saturday the 19th, and A-zone general, the longest general season in the state, closes for good Sunday the 20th. Off in the distance you can already hear the first ducks of the year, and our Dog of the Week is getting ready for exactly that. So this issue points at the buck in front of you and the freezer behind it: a ground venison dinner the whole family will eat, the cooler that keeps him from souring in this heat, and a reader's A-zone buck up top in the Showcase. We also have a new fire on the map close to home and a red flag warning you need to read before you load the truck. Let's get into it.

## The Board: Dates and Deadlines

Tuesday, September 15: dove's first split closes. Two mornings left. The daily limit is 15 mourning and white-winged combined (no more than 10 white-winged), possession triple that, and no limit on Eurasian collared-doves. Shoot time is one half hour before sunrise to sunset. After Tuesday the birds go dark until the second split, November 14 to December 28.

Saturday, September 19: B-zone general opens. B1, B2, B3, B5, and B6 open rifle September 19 to October 25, one buck per tag. B-4 is already running its own earlier general season (August 22 to September 27), and your A-zone tag stays valid during overlap of any B-zone hunt, so you have options this weekend either way. Confirm your exact subzone lines and legal-buck rules in the 2026 Big Game Digest before you climb an unfamiliar ridge.

Sunday, September 20: A-zone general closes. This is your last weekend on the state's longest general season (August 8 to September 20), one buck per tag. Hunt water, feed, and shade at first and last light, and if you fill it, the next two sections are for you.

General bear rides with your deer tag. A-zone general bear has been open since the deer opener and runs to December 27, or closes early if the statewide take hits 1,700 bears. It is non-lead, no bait, no dogs, with tag validation, premolar submission, and reporting all mandatory. A bear tag in your pocket is a second animal on the same hunt.

Looking ahead, ducks are coming. For everyone whose dog is already whining at the back door: the Balance of State duck opener lands Saturday, October 24 (about six weeks out) and runs to January 31, 2027, with a seven-duck daily limit and species sub-limits. The Northeastern Zone opens earlier, around October 3. Now is the week to pull your California Duck Validation, your Federal Duck Stamp, and your free HIP validation, and to confirm the shoot-time tables and final regs at wildlife.ca.gov before opener.

Non-lead, every hunt, no exceptions. Certified non-lead ammunition is required for all firearm hunting anywhere in California, deer and doves alike. And a dove housekeeping reminder while the migratory rules are fresh: plug your shotgun to three shells, get written landowner permission before you hunt private ground, and stay 150 yards off any occupied dwelling.

## From Field to Table: Ground Venison Spaghetti

A lot of you are about to have a freezer full of ground venison, and this is the recipe that earns its keep all winter. It is the weeknight workhorse: a rich red sauce over spaghetti that turns a pound of grind into a dinner the whole family will eat without a word about it being deer. The one trick with venison is that it is lean, almost no fat, so left alone in a pan it cooks up dry and tight. The fix is easy, and it is built into the steps below.

You will need: one pound ground venison (figure a pound for four), olive oil, one diced yellow onion, three to four cloves of garlic minced, one 28-ounce can of crushed tomatoes, two tablespoons of tomato paste, a splash of stock or water, dried oregano and basil (or an Italian blend), a pinch of red pepper flakes, salt and coarse pepper, and one pound of spaghetti. Optional but worth it: a few strips of chopped bacon or a quarter pound of ground pork for fat, a splash of red wine, a pinch of sugar to balance the acid, a parmesan rind, and grated parmesan to finish.

The method:

1. Get some fat in the pan. Venison brings almost none of its own, so start a film of olive oil over medium-high heat, and render the chopped bacon or brown the ground pork first if you are using it. That fat is what keeps the sauce from tasting lean and dry.
1. Brown the venison hard. Add the grind, break it up, and let it actually brown rather than steam. Season with salt and pepper as it goes. Browned meat is where the flavor lives.
1. Build the base. Push the meat aside, add the onion, and cook it soft, then stir in the garlic and the tomato paste and let the paste darken for a minute. If you are using wine, pour it in now and scrape the pan clean.
1. Simmer it down. Add the crushed tomatoes, a splash of stock, the oregano, basil, and red pepper, and a parmesan rind if you have one. Bring it to a bubble, then drop to low and let it simmer 20 to 45 minutes, stirring now and then. Taste and adjust: more salt, and a pinch of sugar if it bites.
1. Marry the pasta. Boil the spaghetti in well-salted water to al dente, save a cup of the pasta water, then drain and toss the noodles right into the sauce with a splash of that water to loosen it. Serve hot with parmesan over the top.

Doneness and safety note: ground venison is the one place we set aside our usual "pink is fine" rule. Grinding folds the surface bacteria all the way through the meat, so cook ground game fully done to 160 degrees, no pink, which is different from the whole-muscle backstrap in Issue #8 that we keep rare on purpose. A long, low simmer takes care of that easily. Wear nitrile gloves when you handle raw grind, and if you ground your own off a fresh buck (Issue #10), keep it cold (Issue #7) right up until it hits the pan.

## Gear Check: The Cooler That Actually Holds Ice

The rule never changes: on a September buck, get the meat cold and keep it cold, because a cooler that melts out by noon is working against you. The Igloo MaxCold Latitude 90-Qt. Roller Cooler is our value pick this week. Ninety quarts swallows a boned-out deer plus ice with room to spare, the foam insulation is rated to hold ice up to five days, and the all-terrain wheels and flip-up tow handle mean you roll a loaded cooler from tailgate to camp instead of wrestling a two-man lift. Floor option: a basic Igloo or Coleman marine cooler for $40 to $70. Step up: a roto-molded RTIC or Yeti for two to three times the money, which holds ice longer and shrugs off abuse but weighs more and has no wheels. Whatever you carry, pre-chill it overnight, pack block ice under your game bags (Issue #3), and keep it in the shade with the drain cracked so meltwater runs off the meat.

## Sunday, September 6, 2026

This is one of those hinge weekends where the calendar does a lot of work at once. Dove is in full swing through the 15th, today is the last light of B-zone archery and archery bear, the A-zone rifle clock is ticking down to the 20th, and the rest of the B zones flip to general in less than two weeks. So this issue is built around the season in front of you: a step-by-step field dressing walkthrough for everyone with a tag to fill, the ear protection you should be wearing on doves and at the sight-in bench, and a first-buck story worth settling in for. We also tagged along on our own opening morning, and we brought the birds home to prove it. Dog of the Week is open this issue, so consider this your nudge to get your hunting partner the shout out he or she deserves. Let's get into it.

## The Board: Dates and Deadlines

Today, September 6: bow season's last light. Archery for B1, B2, B3, B5, and B6 closes today, and statewide archery bear closes today too (August 15 to September 6). If you still have a bow tag in your pocket, this is the evening to fill it. After tonight those zones go quiet until the general opener.

Two weeks out, September 19: B-zone general opens. B1, B2, B3, B5, and B6 open rifle season September 19 and run to October 25, one buck per tag. B-4 runs on its own earlier calendar and is already in its general season, and A-zone tags stay valid during any B-zone hunt, so plan your next two weekends accordingly.

A-zone general closes September 20. You have two weekends left on the state's longest general season (August 8 to September 20), one buck per tag. Hunt water, feed, and shade at first and last light, and confirm your exact subzone lines and legal-buck rules in the 2026 Big Game Digest before you climb an unfamiliar ridge.

Dove is on through September 15. The first split runs to the 15th, then reopens November 14 to December 28. Daily limit is 15 mourning and white-winged combined (no more than 10 white-winged), possession triple that, and no limit on Eurasian collared-doves. Shoot time is one half hour before sunrise to sunset. If you have not been out yet, you still have a week and a half of the early split.

General bear rides with your deer tag. A-zone general bear has been open since the deer opener and runs to December 27, or closes early if the statewide take hits 1,700 bears. It is non-lead, no bait, no dogs, with tag validation, premolar submission, and reporting all mandatory. A bear tag in your pocket is a second animal on the same hunt.

Non-lead, every hunt, no exceptions. Certified non-lead ammunition is required for all firearm hunting anywhere in California, deer and doves alike. And a dove housekeeping reminder while the migratory rules are fresh: plug your shotgun to three shells, get written landowner permission before you hunt private ground, and stay 150 yards off any occupied dwelling.

## From Field to Table: Field Dressing a Buck, Start to Finish (Do Not Leave the Pluck)

This week we are trading the recipe for a field skill, because a lot of you have a deer tag burning a hole in your pocket right now. Back in Issue #12 we ran the gutless method, which is the move when a buck falls a long way from the truck and you are packing him out in pieces. This is the other one: the classic, open-the-cavity field dress you use when you can get the whole animal back to the truck or the cabin. Done right it takes about ten minutes and every organ comes out clean, and the most common rookie mistake is calling it finished before it actually is.

You will need: a sharp knife (the replaceable-blade knife from Issue #4 shines here, no field sharpening), a pair of nitrile gloves, and your game bags (Issue #3) to keep meat off the ground. A short length of paracord to tie back a leg or the bung helps. A small saw is optional, and only for splitting the pelvis if you want to.

The method:

1. Set him up and open the hide. Roll the buck onto his back, head slightly uphill so gravity works for you. Pinch and lift the belly skin, nick through it, then slide two fingers under the blade to guide it and unzip the abdomen from the base of the sternum down to the pelvis. Fingers first, blade shallow: you are opening the wall, not the guts behind it.
1. Cut the diaphragm loose. This is the step first-timers forget most often. The diaphragm is the sheet of muscle that walls the chest off from the belly. Run your knife along the inside of the rib cage on both sides and free it completely, which opens the chest cavity to you.
1. Reach up and take the pluck. Reach as far up into the chest as you can, find the windpipe and esophagus, and cut them off high. Then pull down and back: the heart, lungs, and windpipe (the "pluck") roll out with the whole gut mass in one motion. That is the payoff for cutting the diaphragm. Skip it and everything above the diaphragm stays in the deer, which is exactly how you end up with a problem.
1. Free the back end. Cut a ring around the bung to release the lower intestine, or split the pelvis with your saw and lift the tract out clean. Tie the bung off with a piece of paracord first if you want a tidy job and no mess on the meat.
1. Drain, prop, and cool. Roll the deer on his side to drain the cavity, wipe it out, and prop it open with a clean stick so air moves through. Save the heart and liver if you eat them (worth it). Then get him into the shade and headed for a cooler or a hanging tree, because the clock is already running.

Doneness and safety note: this is field care, not the stove, but the rule that runs this whole newsletter still holds: get it cold and clean. Wear the gloves, and keep the blade off the paunch and bladder so you do not taint the meat. If you do nick one, rinse the area and trim back what it touched. In this early-September heat the spoilage clock starts the second he is down, so cool fast (the rule from Issue #7), then break him down at the table (Issue #10) and match each cut to its plan: tender cuts hot and pink (Issue #8), workhorse cuts low and slow (Issue #11). And if he falls where no truck can reach, that is the day for the gutless method (Issue #12) instead.

## Gear Check: Save Your Ears Without Losing the Field

![](/media/c7986440-e012-4f29-874a-3ae3dea44c5b.png)

Dove season puts a lot of shells through a lot of shotguns, and plenty of you are also at the bench dialing a rifle before the B-zone opener. Every report takes a small, permanent bite out of your hearing. Electronic ear pro fixes the old tradeoff: it clamps down on the muzzle blast while amplifying everything quieter, so you protect your ears and still hear the dog, your buddy, and the birds working in.

Walker's Restrictor Bluetooth Earbuds are our value benchmark. They carry a 24 dB noise reduction rating and use split-second sound-activated compression to kill the shot while passing through wingbeats and normal talk. The earbud shape is the win for hunters: nothing fights your rifle cheek weld the way muffs do, and they tuck under a hat and disappear. Rechargeable, about 14 hours a charge, with Bluetooth and four sound modes through the Walker's Link app. They list near $250 but street closer to $130 to $180, so check current pricing. We ran these on the dove opener ourselves: used and approved by the NorCalHunt team.

Floor option: Walker's Razor Slim electronic muffs run $45 to $60 and protect just as well at the bench, only bulkier in the field. Step up: ISOtunes earbuds or custom-molded digital plugs for two to three times the money. Whatever you pick, wear it on the opener and at the range, and keep a set in the bag with your dove vest (Issue #13).

Check out our running list of gear recommendations at norcalhunt.com/gearecs

## The Showcase

![](/media/1a543bb4-6fbf-410b-b99b-222680424f65.png)

This week we are pulling back the curtain on our own opening morning. The NorCalHunt crew got out for the September 1 dove opener and put in the work, and here is the honest report: we did not limit out, but we brought home a solid strap of birds. That is most opening days, and it beats the couch every time.

The best one each week runs up top, and at the end of every month subscribers vote for a Showcase winner and a permanent spot on our subscribers-only Showcase page at norcalhunt.com/showcase.

## Dog of the Week

This week, the spotlight is yours.

We are handing Dog of the Week back to you for one issue: get your hunting partner the shout out he or she has earned. Everybody on this list has a dog worth bragging on, the pointer that finally held steady, the retriever that will not quit the cold water, the mutt that outworks them all. We want to meet yours.

Hit reply, send us a clean photo of your hunting partner, and give us a quick 2 to 3 sentence blurb on what they hunt and where they earn their kibble. Tell us how you want to be credited, and we run first name, last initial, and town. Pointers, flushers, retrievers, and the occasional very good mutt all qualify. Send one in and yours runs right here next week. Want to see who has made the cut so far? Catch up on every dog we have featured on our past Dogs of the Week page at norcalhunt.com/dogoftheweek.

## From the Field: A First Buck, and the Two Old Brothers Who Made the Morning

"Most people will never forget their first hunt, but I reckon I have a better story than most."

It was deer season in the mountains, and a first-timer had drawn into a hunt with the old men: his grandfather, his great uncle, and an old friend of his father's, all of them with more seasons behind them than the boy had years. Days of nothing but sign. Then, from the truck, one word from his grandfather: "Deer." What followed was everything a first hunt is: a scramble out the door without his jacket, one round fumbled into the rifle, a shot that took a foreleg instead of the heart, and a second shot from his grandfather's borrowed rifle that somehow, against every odd, put the buck down.

Then came the field dressing, watched a hundred times and never once done alone, and two old men who answered "not yet" every time the boy asked if he was finished, right up until they did not. What he left inside that deer, and how the two brothers reacted once they got back to the cabin, is the part we would not dream of spoiling.

Submitted by Devon A. of Chico

## Sunday, August 30, 2026

Welcome back. This is the last briefing before the birds fly. Dove opens Tuesday, September 1, just two days out, so this week we point everything at the opener: a bacon-wrapped popper that turns a pile of breasts into the best reason to host the tailgate, the value dove vest that keeps your shells up front and your birds cooling in back, and the paperwork you cannot walk into the field without. A-zone rifle rolls into week four, the bow zones are down to their last weekend, and we have a plate of poppers in the Showcase, a young pointer already holding steady, and a father-son dove hunt that ended with something none of us will ever pull off twice. Let's get into it.

## The Board: Crucial Dates and Deadlines

Tuesday, September 1: dove opener, two days out. The first split runs September 1 to 15. The daily limit is 15 mourning and white-winged doves combined (no more than 10 white-winged), with the possession limit triple that. There is no limit on Eurasian collared-doves. Shoot time is one half hour before sunrise to sunset.

Do the paperwork today, not at 5 a.m. Tuesday. You need your HIP validation (free) and your Upland Game Bird Validation on your license before opening morning. HIP is the single most-missed step on opener day, so knock it out this weekend.

Know the migratory bird rules. Doves are federally regulated migratory birds, so your shotgun has to be plugged to three total shells. On top of that: written landowner permission before you hunt private ground, and no shooting within 150 yards of an occupied dwelling.

A-zone general is in week four. The rifle season runs August 8 to September 20, one buck per tag, one of the longest general seasons in the state. Hunt water, feed, and shade at first and last light, and confirm your exact subzone lines and legal-buck rules in the 2026 Big Game Digest before you climb an unfamiliar ridge.

Last call for B-zone archery. B1, B2, B3, B5, and B6 archery closes September 6, so next weekend is your last for bow season in those zones. B-4 general is in week two (August 22 to September 27), and the rest of the B zones do not open general until September 19.

Archery bear runs through September 6. It is open across the entire bear hunt area on the same first and last light you are already hunting for deer. General bear is already in for A-zone. Non-lead, no bait, no dogs, with tag validation, premolar submission, and reporting all mandatory.

Non-lead, every hunt, no exceptions. Certified non-lead ammunition is required for all firearm hunting anywhere in California, doves included. The useful loads thin out on the shelf the closer we get to Tuesday, so buy your dove shells now while you can still pick your load.

## From Field to Table: Bacon-Wrapped Dove Poppers

Everybody argues about how to cook a dove. This is the recipe that ends the argument. It is the classic tailgate popper, and it is the reason half the people at the field edge are not really there for the shooting. Breast your birds out (two clean fillets off the breastbone per dove, no plucking required), and you are most of the way there.

You will need:

- Boneless dove breasts, 2 fillets per bird, figure 3 to 4 birds per person
- Sliced jalapenos, seeds and ribs removed for less heat, left in for more
- Cream cheese, softened
- Thin-cut bacon, one slice cut in half per popper
- Toothpicks, soaked in water so they do not burn
- Salt, coarse pepper, and any rub you like
- Optional: a splash of Italian dressing or a quick soy-and-garlic soak for an hour first

The method:

1. Season and rest. Pat the breasts dry, salt and pepper them, and let them sit while you prep the rest. Dry meat browns and takes on smoke.
1. Build the stack. Lay a jalapeno slice on each breast, add a small dab of cream cheese, and press a second breast on top like a sandwich, or fold one breast around the filling.
1. Wrap and pin. Wrap a half slice of bacon around the whole thing and run a soaked toothpick through to hold it. Snug, not strangled.
1. Grill hot and fast. Medium-high, lid down, turning to crisp the bacon on all sides. You are cooking to render the bacon and warm the center, roughly 8 to 12 minutes depending on your fire.
1. Pull them at pink. The bacon is your timer: when it is crisp, the dove is done. Rest two minutes and serve.

Doneness and safety note: dove breast is dark, lean meat that eats best hot and fast with a warm pink center, the same principle behind that backstrap in Issue #8. Cook it past that and it turns dry and livery, which is where doves get their bad reputation. If you would rather cook birds to a fully done, no-pink center, drop the poppers into a covered braise instead and let them go low and slow. Two housekeeping rules that matter more in September heat than any recipe: wear a pair of nitrile gloves when you clean birds and wash up after, and get your doves onto ice in the field, not on a hot tailgate, the same cool-fast rule we hammered back in Issue #7.

## Gear Check: Keep Shells Up Front and Birds Cooling in Back

MidwayUSA Men's Dove Vest

![](/media/1f0ee613-c30c-4cb5-aa8c-453a4988587a.png)

On the opener you stand a field edge for hours in the heat, and a good vest earns its keep three ways: shells within reach, a spot for your license, water, and phone, and a mesh game bag that keeps your birds off your sweaty back. The mesh is the point. It breathes while you shoot and drains and airs your birds while you walk, which buys you time before they hit the cooler.

The value benchmark is the MidwayUSA Dove Vest: a prewashed cotton-poly twill body with mesh front, sides, and back, external shell loops that hold their shape, roomy cargo pockets, and a large blood-proof game bag. It runs around $30 to $40, so check current pricing and stock.

Floor option: a simple dove belt or shell pouch with a mesh game bag, around $20 to $30. The Bug Fire on the Lassen and Sierra county line sits around 93,700 acres and roughly 97 percent contained, deep into mop-up, and the MP18 Fire near Hoopa in Humboldt County is around 7,600 acres and about three-quarters contained, with evacuations rolled back to warnings. Do not read that as all-clear, though. The nation is still at Preparedness Level 5, the highest there is, which means firefighting crews and aircraft are stretched thin and a new start today will not draw the same fast response it would have in June. CAL FIRE's Northern California outlook calls for warmer-than-normal inland temperatures and occasional thunderstorms into September, and that thunder is the real risk: dry lightning on cured grass is how the next big one begins. Before you load the truck:

Confirm restrictions for your unit. Closures and burn bans change fast and vary by district. Check fire.ca.gov and with your local forest before you go.

Watch the sky, not just the ground. If you hear thunder or see build-ups, rethink a long push into dry timber. Lightning is the ignition you cannot control.

Do not be the ignition. No sparks near dry grass, and mind your exhaust and your drag chains. At PL5, one careless moment costs more than it ever has.

Beat the heat, on birds and bucks alike. Hunt first and last light, carry more water than you think you need, and get doves on ice and any downed deer cooled fast before the meat sours.

Stay safe out there, get your gear cleaned, and we'll see you in the field.

The NorCal Hunt Team
