issues.body:
Sunday, August 23, 2026

Welcome back. A-zone rifle is into its third week, B-4 became the first B zone to open its general season yesterday, and dove is now nine days out. So this week we go deep, into the country most hunters glass but never walk into, because that is where the mature bucks live and where a filled tag turns into real work. We put the value-benchmark meat-hauling frame pack on your back, walk through the gutless method to turn a downed buck into pack-ready loads without ever opening the gut, and meet a 14-year-old pointer who still locks up like a statue. The poll is in too, and it confirms what we already suspected about how most of us got here. Let's get into it.

## The Board: Crucial Dates and Deadlines

- A-zone general is in week three. The rifle season runs August 8 to September 20, one buck per tag, one of the longest general seasons in the state. Deer are locked into a late-summer pattern, so hunt water, feed, and shade at first and last light. Confirm your exact subzone lines and legal-buck rules in the 2026 Big Game Digest before you climb an unfamiliar ridge.
- Yesterday, August 22: B-4 general opened. B-4 is the first B zone to open its rifle season, running August 22 to September 27. The rest of the B zones (B1, B2, B3, B5, B6) do not open general until September 19. Remember that a B tag is valid in any B zone during either the archery or the general season, so you can be in B-4 with a rifle right now, or stay in the bow woods elsewhere. Confirm your exact subzone dates either way.
- B-zone archery is still open. B1, B2, B3, B5, and B6 run archery August 15 to September 6. That is two more weekends of bow season before those close.
- Archery bear runs through September 6. It is open across the entire bear hunt area, on the same first and last light you are already hunting for deer, so a bear tag in your pocket is a second animal for free. It is non-lead, no bait, no dogs, with tag validation, premolar submission, and reporting all mandatory. General bear is already in for A-zone and runs to December 27, or closes early if the statewide harvest hits 1,700 bears (last year's take was around 1,180, so an early close is unlikely).
- Nine days out, September 1: dove opener. The first split runs September 1 to 15. The daily limit is 15 mourning and white-winged doves combined (no more than 10 white-winged), with the possession limit triple that. There is no limit on Eurasian collared-doves. Do the boring paperwork this week: you need your HIP validation (free) and your Upland Game Bird Validation on your license before opening morning. HIP is the single most-missed step on opener day, so get it now, not in the dark at 5 a.m. on the 1st.
- Non-lead, every hunt, no exceptions. Certified non-lead ammunition is required for all firearm hunting anywhere in California, doves included. The useful loads thin out on the shelf as each opener lands, so buy your rifle boxes and your dove shells now while you can still pick what you want.

## From Field to Table: The Gutless Method (Quarter a Buck Where He Falls)

A frame pack (see the Gear Check below) is only worth carrying if you can turn a whole deer into loads you can strap to it. The gutless method does exactly that. It takes every major cut of meat off the animal without ever opening the body cavity, which means no gut pile to work around, less mess, and meat that stays cleaner. It is the move for any buck that falls a long way from the truck, and it sets up the kitchen-table breakdown we covered in Issue #10.

You will need: a sharp knife (the replaceable-blade knife from Issue #4 is ideal, so you are swapping blades instead of field-sharpening), your game bags (Issue #3), a short length of paracord to hold a leg back, and a clean surface or the inside of a game bag to lay meat on. Keep the meat out of the dirt.

The method:

1. Skin the up side only. Roll the deer onto its side. Cut down the spine from the base of the neck to the tail, and peel the hide down the side facing up to expose the shoulder, the backstrap, and the hindquarter. You are only skinning half the deer for now.
1. Take the front shoulder. There is no ball joint here. The front leg is held on by muscle alone. Lift the leg, cut between the shoulder blade and the ribs, and it lifts free. Into a game bag.
1. Lift the backstrap. Run the knife along one side of the spine from neck to hip, then along the tops of the ribs, and peel the whole loin off in one long piece. This is your best meat, so take your time and stay tight to the bone.
1. Free the hindquarter. Cut around the ball joint at the hip and work the entire hindquarter off the pelvis. Bag it as one bone-in quarter, or bone it out right there to shave weight off your pack.
1. Get the neck and the tenderloins. Trim the neck meat and any rib and flank trim you want (grind and braise gold). Then reach up inside along the lower spine, behind the last rib, for the tenderloins on the underside. They sit inside the cavity, but you can pull them without ever gutting the animal.
1. Roll and repeat. Flip the deer and do the same on the other side. When you are finished, all the meat is in bags and the carcass is intact.

Doneness and safety note: this is field care, not cooking, but the rule that runs this whole newsletter still applies: get the meat cold and clean. Keep each bag off the hide and out of the dirt, get air moving around the quarters, and in this late-August heat get everything into the shade and headed downhill fast, because the spoilage clock starts the second the animal is down. Once it is home, break it down at the table (Issue #10) and match each cut to its plan: tender cuts hot and pink (Issue #8), workhorse cuts low and slow (Issue #11).

## Gear Check: Carry the Whole Deer on Your Back

ALPS OutdoorZ Commander + Pack Bag

![](/media/62dbdfa0-469e-4a8e-b8d8-7b9a074ca94d.png)

Once the buck is quartered and bagged, the hunt becomes a hauling job, and that is where deep country humbles a cheap pack. A true meat-hauling frame rides the load low and tight against your hips instead of dragging it off your shoulders, so you can walk heavy, awkward quarters out of a canyon without wrecking your back on the first trip.

The value benchmark is the ALPS OutdoorZ Commander. You get a 5,250 cubic inch pack bag to haul gear and camp in, and when the bag comes off, an aluminum freighter frame with a load shelf and a lashing system built to strap quarters down tight. The torso adjusts from 17 to 23 inches, there is a rifle holder and a spotting scope pocket, and it ships with three extension straps for when the load gets ugly. Hunters routinely pack whole deer, and even elk quarters, out with it.

It runs around $180 to $220 for the frame-plus-bag system, and you can buy the freighter frame on its own for less if you already have a day pack you like, so check current pricing and stock. Know the tradeoff going in: it is an external frame, so it is a little bulky in tight timber and it has no load-lifter straps. That is the price you pay for the price you pay. Step up to an internal-frame hauler like the Mystery Ranch Metcalf for a sleeker carry if you have the budget (expect two to three times the money). Floor option: strip the bag off and run just the frame.

Pair it with your game bags (Issue #3) and the replaceable-blade knife (Issue #4): quarter with the gutless method above, bag the meat, lash it to the shelf, and walk it out. This is the piece of gear that makes hunting the deep stuff possible instead of just a good idea.

## The Showcase

This week's feature: a dove hunter's dream on video. A NorCalHunt subscriber out of Glenn County sent us a clip of doves working a freshly cut safflower field, dropping in to feed by the dozen. It is a heck of a scouting lesson too: find the fresh-cut fields as the opener nears and you find the birds.

![](/media/02768477-33ca-4648-8291-9c2b6bc57c66.jpg)

(Full clip on our YouTube channel and Showcase page, links below.)

The best one each week runs up top, and at the end of every month subscribers vote for a Showcase winner. Every pick earns a permanent spot on our subscribers-only Showcase page at norcalhunt.com/showcase. Send us one to keep it rolling.

## Dog of the Week

![](/media/fa6907b2-8d1d-4412-885f-3af7a4c59661.jpg)

Meet "Hayden" Owner: Allen C., Forest Ranch

Hayden is 14 years old and still doing the one thing she was born to do. In this week's photo she is locked up on a pheasant, tail high and nose full, as steady on point as she was a decade ago. A German shorthaired pointer's drive does not retire on a schedule, and Hayden is proof that the best old dogs never lose a step where it counts. Fourteen seasons in, she has earned every soft bed and every slow walk back to the truck.

Some of the best hunts of the year are happening right now, and this spot is wide open for yours.

Everybody on this list has at least one. The buck that stepped out with two minutes of light left. The pack-out that had you questioning your life choices somewhere around midnight. issues.title: A first buck, two brothers, and one last hunt
issues.blurb: Plus the venison cut most hunters give to the grinder, the rest we swear by, and dove opener two weeks out.
issues.body:
Sunday, August 16, 2026

Welcome back. The season is in full swing now. A-zone rifle is into its second week, and a few more doors opened yesterday on August 15: B-zone and C-zone archery, plus archery bear. Last week you told us in the poll that steaks and roasts are where most of your deer ends up, so this week we do right by the roast, the low-and-slow way that turns even a tough cut into the best pot roast of the winter. We put a rock-solid, one-hand shooting rest in your hands, meet a camp dog who never got the hunting memo, and share a story about a first buck, two old brothers, and one last morning at deer camp. Let's get into it.

## The Board: Crucial Dates and Deadlines

- A-zone general is in week two. The A-zone general (rifle) season runs August 8 to September 20, one buck per tag, one of the longest general seasons in the state. Deer are settling into a late-summer pattern: first and last light around water, feed, and shade. Confirm your exact subzone lines and either-sex rules in the 2026 Big Game Digest before you climb a new ridge.
- August 15: B-zone archery is open. Most of the B zones (B1, B2, B3, B5, B6) run archery August 15 to September 6. B-zone tags are valid in any B zone during either season, so confirm your exact subzone dates before you commit.
- Today, August 16: B-4 archery closes. The early bird of the B zones, open since July 25, shuts tonight. If you are carrying a B tag and want a bow hunt this weekend, this is your last day in B-4.
- August 15: C-zone archery (Hunt A-1) opened too. Archery in the northeastern C zones (Modoc, Lassen, Siskiyou, Shasta) runs only on a drawn Hunt A-1 tag, and standard archery-only tags are not valid there. All four subzones opened August 15 and run into late August or early September, and the general C-zone rifle season then opens September 19. Closing dates vary by subzone, so confirm your exact dates and boundaries in the 2026 Big Game Digest.
- August 15: archery bear opened too. Archery bear runs August 15 to September 6 across the entire bear hunt area. General bear is already in for A-zone (it opened with the August 8 deer opener) and runs through December 27, or closes early if the statewide harvest hits 1,700 bears. It is non-lead, no bait, no dogs, and tag validation, premolar submission, and reporting are all mandatory. Glass the same first and last light you are already hunting for deer and you may fill two tags on one trip.
- Two weeks out, September 1: dove opener. The first split runs September 1 to 15. The daily limit is 15 mourning and white-winged doves combined (no more than 10 white-winged), with the possession limit triple that. No limit on Eurasian collared-doves. Do the boring paperwork now: you need your HIP validation (free) and your Upland Game Bird Validation on your license before opening morning. HIP is the most-missed step on opener day. Get it in August, not in the dark at 5 a.m. on September 1.
- Non-lead, every hunt, no exceptions. Certified non-lead ammunition is required for all hunting with a firearm anywhere in California, doves included. The useful loads thin out on the shelf as every opener lands, so buy your rifle boxes and your dove shells now, while you can still pick what you want.

## From Field to Table: The Low-and-Slow Braise (Turn a Tough Roast Tender)

You told us last week that steaks and roasts are where most of your deer ends up. Here is the catch nobody warns you about: not every roast wants to be cooked the same way. The tender cuts (backstrap, tenderloin, top round) reward fast, hot, and pink, the way we cooked that backstrap back in Issue #8. The workhorse cuts you separated out last week (bottom round, rump, shank, shoulder, and neck) are full of connective tissue that stays like a rubber band if you cook it fast and turns to silk if you cook it low and slow. This is the other half of the animal, and it is the best cold-weather eating you own.

You will need:

- 2 to 3 lbs venison roast from a tough cut (bottom round, rump, shoulder, or a couple of shanks), silver skin trimmed
- Salt, coarse black pepper, and a little oil for searing
- 1 onion, 2 carrots, a rib or two of celery, a few garlic cloves
- 2 to 3 cups liquid: beef or game stock, plus a splash of red wine if you have it
- A couple of bay leaves and a sprig of thyme or rosemary
- Optional: a spoonful of tomato paste for body

The method:

1. Dry and season. Pat the roast bone-dry and salt it well all over. Dry meat browns. Wet meat just steams.
1. Sear hard. Get a Dutch oven or heavy pot hot with a little oil and brown the roast on every side. That deep crust is where most of the flavor comes from, so do not rush it.
1. Build the base. Pull the meat out, drop the heat, and soften the onion, carrot, celery, and garlic in the drippings. Stir in the tomato paste if you are using it and let it darken a minute, then deglaze with the wine or a splash of stock, scraping the browned bits off the bottom.
1. Braise low and slow. Return the roast, add stock until it comes about two-thirds of the way up the meat (not fully covered), tuck in the herbs and bay, and bring it to a bare simmer. Lid on, then hold it low: stovetop on low, a 300 degree oven, or a slow cooker on low. Give it time, usually 3 to 4 hours, until a fork twists in the meat with no resistance.
1. Do not chase pink here. This is the one venison cut where pink is not the goal. A braise is finished when the connective tissue has broken down and the meat pulls apart, well past medium. Cooked past done, on purpose, is the whole point.
1. Rest, then pull or slice. Skim the fat, reduce the liquid into a gravy if you want one, and serve it over mashed potatoes, egg noodles, or polenta.

Doneness and safety note: braising carries the meat well past the 160 degree mark, so safety takes care of itself here. The finish line is texture, not temperature: fork-tender, falling apart, silky. This is the counterpart to the fast, hot, pink sear you save for the tender cuts (Issue #8), and it is exactly where the shank and bottom round from last week's breakdown (Issue #10) were always headed. Leftovers cool and freeze beautifully, so a big roast today is two dinners in December.

## Gear Check: A Steady Rest for the Shot That Counts

Primos Trigger Stick Gen 3 Tripod

![](/media/8732609d-0e0d-4887-b289-baf89605d68a.png)

When the moment finally comes, a clean shot often comes down to one thing: how steady you are. Offhand shots in close country get rushed, and a rushed shot is how a good hunt turns into a long day of tracking. A solid rest takes the wobble out and lets you put the bullet exactly where it belongs, the first time.

The Trigger Stick is the value benchmark here. Squeeze the trigger grip and the tripod raises or drops to your height with one hand, so you can go from glassing to a locked-in rest without fumbling or standing up. It works sitting, kneeling, or standing, the V-yoke pops off so you can mount a spotting scope or binoculars on the same legs, and it pans smoothly to track a moving buck. For the close, brushy A-zone and B-zone country where shots come fast and offhand, it turns a shaky standing shot into a supported one.

This is a piece of gear the NorCalHunt team swears by. If you have the space to pack it, you will not regret it when it comes down to the moment it is time to pull the trigger.

## The Showcase

![](/media/419c46b2-c58c-4b4e-ae7b-3afd17156a01.png)

This week's Showcase is a look behind the curtain from our own crew. It is a duck patch in Glenn County, mowed down low with one thing left standing: a few green patches of duckweed. That is not neglect, that is the plan. Everything else got knocked down so the birds have a clean table and the duckweed can do its work, because that green stuff is exactly the kind of food ducks pile in on once the water goes back over it. Right now it is just a quiet patch of green in the August heat. Come flood-up, it is a spot with a job to do. This is what prep season looks like, months before the first bird ever drops into the decoys.

The Showcase runs on you, and it is exclusive to subscribers, so the people on this list are the only ones who see it. Grip-and-grins, a limit strap in the fog, the dog mid-retrieve, a kid's first bird, a velvet giant on your summer cameras, or a scouting shot like this one. If it is part of your season, we want it. Every pick earns a permanent spot on our subscribers-only Showcase page at norcalhunt.com/showcase.

To get in: hit reply with your photo or clip and a sentence about it, and tell us how you want to be credited (we run first name, last initial, and town). The best one each week runs up top, and at the end of every month subscribers vote for a Showcase winner. Send us one to keep it rolling.

## Dog of the Week

![](/media/91dd67f0-cfa9-4a29-8760-eb8cc1174fd7.png)

Meet "Tucker" Owner: Mike W., Durham

Tucker is a five-year-old red border collie, and no, he was not bred to hunt. He is proof that your best hunting companion does not have to come from a line of bird dogs. He spends most of his days being a loyal partner and chasing light reflections around the house. Not every good dog earns a spot in the blind, and Tucker is a reminder that the one riding shotgun to camp counts just as much.

Want your dog featured? Hit reply, send us a clean photo of your hunting partner, and give us a quick 2 to 3 sentence blurb on what they hunt and where they earn their kibble. Pointers, flushers, retrievers, and the occasional very good mutt all qualify.

Missed a week? Catch up on every dog we have featured on our past Dogs of the Week page at norcalhunt.com/dogoftheweek.

## From the Field: A Buck, Two Brothers, and One Last Hunt

"Some hunts grow more valuable with age."

It was late deer season in the G1 zone, the kind of Northern California morning that bites at dawn and warms enough by afternoon to make you shed a jacket. A young hunter was up in the hills with two men who had spent more years in deer country than he had been alive: his grandpa, Pops, and his great-uncle Floyd. Two old brothers who knew the country, knew deer, and knew how to help a kid get his first buck without ever taking the hunt away from him. There was a .30-30, a big forked horn, a first shot that went low, and three quiet words as Pops handed over his .270: take your time.

Back at camp, bacon was frying. What none of them knew that morning was that it was the last time those two brothers would ever hunt together. Years later, it is not the antlers that stay with the man who tells it. It is Floyd's pickup, Pops' .270, and two old men passing along what they knew to the next generation.

Contributor: Alex A., Chico

Read the full story on norcalhunt.com/fieldstories.

Got a hunt that turned into a story? A first buck, a close call, a last morning with people you have since lost? Hit reply and tell us. The best ones run right here.

Last week's poll is in. We asked where the meat goes when you break down a deer, and steaks and roasts took the top spot, with straight-to-grind coming in second. Still hot, dry, and primed to burn. California sat at Preparedness Level 5, the highest there is, into mid-August, with a heat wave and critically dry fuels. No major fire in our deer country right now, but the real risk is a thunderstorm dropping fresh lightning on cured grass. Before you load the truck:

## Sunday, August 9, 2026

Welcome back. The countdown is over. The A-zone rifle opener hit yesterday, and for the first time this year the biggest general deer season in the state is live under our boots. If you were out there this morning, you already know the difference a hard-horned buck makes. This week we pick up right where a filled tag leaves off: how to break down a hindquarter at the kitchen table by following the seams. Then we look three weeks down the road to the dove opener with the one decoy that pulls passing birds into range. We have got a velvet buck in the Showcase from one of you and a five-year-old bird dog caught on a pheasant retrieve. We are also pausing this week to celebrate a hometown crew that just made NorCal proud on the national stage. Plus a straight read on the fire and heat picture before you head back out. Let's get into it.

## The Board: Crucial Dates and Deadlines

- Saturday, August 8: A-zone general is OPEN. The rifle opener is behind us and the season is on. A-zone general runs August 8 to September 20, a 44-day stretch that is among the longest general deer seasons in California. One buck per tag. The first days, before pressure pushes deer nocturnal, are some of your best odds all season, so hunt hard early. Confirm your exact subzone dates and either-sex rules in the 2026 Big Game Digest before you go.
- August 8: general bear came in with the deer. General bear opens concurrently with the general deer opener in A-zone, so if you are carrying a bear tag you can hunt it right now alongside your blacktail. Non-lead, no bait, no dogs, with validation and reporting mandatory.
- Saturday, August 15: B-zone archery and archery bear both open. Most B zones (B1, B2, B3, B5, B6) run archery August 15 to September 6. Archery bear opens the same day across the entire bear hunt area. Confirm your exact B subzone dates in the Digest before you commit.
- August 16: B-4 archery closes. The early bird of the B zones (open since July 25) shuts on the 16th. This is your last weekend for B-4 bow.
- Leftover deer tags are still on the board. Unclaimed premium tags have been on first-come, first-served sale since August 2. If you struck out in the draw, this is a real second shot. Log into your CDFW online sales profile and check availability, because the good ones move fast.
- Looking ahead, September 1: dove opener. First split runs September 1 to 15. Daily bag is 15 mourning and white-winged doves combined, up to 10 of which may be white-winged. Two things to grab now and not at 5 a.m. on opening morning: your free HIP validation and your Upland Game Bird Validation. More on doves as it gets closer.
- Non-lead, every hunt, no exceptions. Certified non-lead ammunition is required for all hunting with a firearm anywhere in California, doves included. The right loads thin out on the shelf as each opener lands, so buy ahead while you can still pick your load.

## Spotlight: Durham High Trap Team

![](/media/42870907-531e-4e19-a6e7-af23eed9bdaf.png)

Pictured left to right: Rowan Turnquist., Hank Simmons., Adam Simpson., Jacob Hayes., and Jake Dunlap.

We are stepping out of the field for a minute to brag on some of our own. The NorCalHunt team wants to shine the spotlight on the Durham High trap shooting team for a season worth celebrating, capped by winning the United States Open Youth Clay Shooting Sports Championships in Las Vegas. Not only did Durham win 1st in team points, but our very own Adam Simpson took the 1st place individual title at Nationals. That is a long road from Durham, CA, and a whole lot of clays broken along the way, and these young shooters earned every bit of it with the skill, focus, and discipline the sport demands. Congratulations to the whole squad, their families, and coaches Allen Cornelison and Dylan Dunlap for getting them there. Durham is proud of you, and so is NorCalHunt.

## From Field to Table: Break Down a Hindquarter

Say you connected this weekend. You hung and skinned the buck at the truck (that hoist from Issue 9), kept it cold on the drive home (Issue 7), and now the whole hindquarter is sitting on your counter. Here is the good news: that big, intimidating chunk of meat is really just four or five separate muscles held together by thin sheets of silverskin. You do not need a bone saw and you do not need to be a butcher. You need a sharp knife and a willingness to follow the seams.

You will need: a thin, flexible boning or fillet knife, a clean and sanitized surface, well-chilled meat, a bowl for trim, and your game bags or vacuum bags for packaging.

The method:

1. Start cold and clean. Work chilled meat on a sanitized surface, and keep your hands, board, and knife clean the whole way through. Cold meat is firmer, easier to handle, and safer.
1. Follow the seams. The hindquarter splits into its muscle groups along natural silverskin membranes. Work your fingers and the tip of your knife into those seams and let the muscles come apart with almost no cutting. You are separating, not sawing.
1. Know what each piece is. The main players are the top round (inside round, the biggest and one of the better ones), the bottom round (outside round, a touch tougher), the eye of round (small and uniform), the sirloin tip or knuckle, and the top sirloin up near the hip. Down at the shank is the lower leg.
1. Match the cut to the plan. Top round and sirloin become steaks or a roast. Bottom round and eye of round are perfect for jerky (that recipe from Issue 9). The shank and every odd scrap go to grind or to a low, slow braise.
1. Shave the silverskin. Peel the silver connective tissue off each muscle before you package it. It never breaks down and cooks up like a rubber band, so angle your blade up toward the skin and shave it clean.
1. Package by use. Label everything, seal it, and portion your grind into flat one-pound bricks so it freezes fast and stacks like books.

Doneness and safety note: keep everything cold and clean and get it into the fridge or freezer promptly. Whole-muscle cuts like steaks and roasts eat best cooked to a warm pink, medium-rare center, but anything you grind should be cooked to an internal 160 degrees, because grinding mixes any surface bacteria all the way through. And if you saved the two tenderloins from inside the cavity, treat those like backstrap and pull them pink (Issue 8).

## Gear Check: Put Motion Over Your Dove Field

![](/media/c9410fa0-f1f8-450a-a110-57990c78d806.png)

MOJO Voodoo Dove

The dove opener is three weeks out, and nothing pulls passing birds like motion. Doves cue on other doves, and a spinning-wing decoy on a field edge reads as a bird dropping in to feed. Set one where you want birds to cross, and you can turn an empty field corner into a shoot.

The pick is the MOJO Voodoo Dove, the current version of the decoy that more or less invented motion dove hunting. You get a realistic body in the landing position, magnetic spinning wings (no fiddly thumb screws), a steel support pole, and up to 16 hours on 4 AA batteries, so it runs sunrise to sunset. It goes for around $45, often less per unit in a two-pack (check current pricing). Bring spare AA batteries, because the wings quit spinning before you notice.

Step-up options: run two spinners on opposite edges to work birds from more directions, or move up to the heavier-duty MOJO Elite Series dove. Floor option: a four-pack of clip-on stationary dove decoys (about $20) set on a fence wire or a bare branch builds a spread around the spinner for pocket change.

One California note worth having straight: motorized dove spinners are legal for the September dove opener. The catch is that some CDFW wildlife areas and refuges restrict electronic/motorized decoys on public land, so verify the rules for your specific ground before you set up. And non-lead shot is required for dove, statewide. On a hot opener, breast and cool your birds fast, the same cold-fast principle we covered back in Issue 7.

## The Showcase

![](/media/6d57949b-a66e-4df0-ad18-26020628dba2.png)

The calendar is turning fast, and this week's Showcase caught it mid-turn. Tad A. of Durham sent in a photo of a buck still carrying a full set of velvet antlers, soft and swollen and still growing. Last week we saw one raking his velvet off in the brush. Tad's buck is the before picture: the last quiet days before the antlers harden, the velvet strips, and every deer on your summer cameras turns into a different animal by the opener. If you are still running cameras, you are watching this exact clock tick down.

That is what the Showcase runs on: you. It is exclusive to subscribers, so the people on this list are the only ones who see it. ## Dog of the Week

![](/media/b1d92b9c-6739-4774-8c7d-89f615f4869a.png)

Meet "Amaya" Owner: Allen C. Forest Ranch, CA

Amaya is a five-year-old German shorthaired pointer, all nose and drive in the uplands. Allen caught her on a pheasant retrieve in this week's photo, doing exactly what the breed was built for. Five seasons in, she has the job down cold, and with dove three weeks out and pheasant behind it, she has a busy fall ahead.

Last week's poll is in. We asked how you were getting ready for your opener, and the winner was clear: locked and loaded, just counting down. Scouting and glassing, getting zeroed, and sorting gear and tags all pulled votes, but the biggest share of you had the work behind you and were simply watching the calendar tick toward your season opener. Well, the wait is over. The counting down turned into opening morning, and judging by the photos already hitting our inbox, plenty of you made it count.

This week's poll ties right to today's Field to Table. Now that the season is on and meat is coming home, where does most of your deer end up?

### When you break down a deer, where does the meat go?

Got a hunting partner who lives in the foothills, the rice, or along the riverbanks? Forward this briefing and point them to norcalhunt.com. Word of mouth from real hunters is how we grow.

## Conditions: Heat and Fire, Read This Before You Head Back Out

NorCal is hot and dry and the fire picture is active heading into opening week. The biggest one near our southern edge right now is the Gann Fire in Calaveras County, near New Hogan Lake. It pushed past 10,000 acres midweek with early containment lines going in, evacuation orders in place around the lake, and a suspect already arrested on suspicion of recklessly causing it. Add a triple-digit heat wave and smoke drifting in from out-of-state fires, and CAL FIRE keeps large-fire potential above normal through the summer. Conditions move fast, so check current status before you load the truck.

- Confirm restrictions for your exact unit. Forest Service, BLM, and CAL FIRE rules change fast and vary by district, so check your specific ground before you go.
- Do not be the ignition. No sparks near dry grass, and mind your exhaust and drag chains. The Gann Fire is the reminder: one careless moment can burn 10,000 acres and end in cuffs.
- Watch the air. Smoke and poor air quality can roll in fast. Check the AQI before a hard climb, especially if you are packing a buck out in the heat.
- Beat the heat. Hunt the first and last hour around water and shade, carry more water than you think you need, and cool any deer immediately. In this heat, a downed buck is a race.

Stay safe out there, get your gear cleaned, and we'll see you in the field.

The NorCal Hunt Team

issues.body:
## Sunday, August 2, 2026

Welcome back. Today is a hinge in the season: this morning is the last day of Zone A archery, and next Saturday the rifle opener puts the biggest, longest deer season in the state on the board. Here is what is riding along over the next six days. We turn the back of the freezer into field food with a batch of venison jerky, square away a truck-hitch hoist so you can hang and skin a buck by yourself, and go live with the very first Showcase photo, a velvet buck one of you caught on video. Dog of the Week is a two-dog team you will want to meet, From the Field is a goose-morning reunion that stuck with the hunter who lived it, and this week's poll wants to know how you are getting ready for your opener. Let's get into it.

## The Board: Crucial Dates and Deadlines

- Today, August 2, is the last day of Zone A archery. The coastal blacktail archery season (July 11 to August 2) closes tonight. If you are chasing a buck with a bow, this is your last morning until the rifle season opens. After today, A-zone goes quiet for five days before the general opener.
- Today, August 2: leftover premium deer tags go on sale. Unclaimed premium tags, the ones that went unpaid or unallocated after the draw, are released on a first-come, first-served basis starting the first Week of August. If you struck out in the main draw, this is a real second shot at a good tag. Log into your CDFW online sales profile and check availability early, because the good ones move fast.
- Saturday, August 8: Zone A general (rifle) opener. This is the big one. A-zone general runs August 8 to September 20, one of the longest general seasons in the state at 44 days. One buck per tag. Three things to handle this week, not Friday night: confirm your 2026-27 license and tags are current, pattern your certified non-lead load and get zeroed, and confirm your exact subzone dates and either-sex rules in the 2026 Big Game Digest. A-zone splits into units and you want to be standing on the right line.
- Bear comes in with the deer. General bear opens concurrently with the general deer opener in zones A, B, C, D, X8, X9A, X9B, X10, and X12, so in A-zone you can carry a bear tag on the August 8 opener. Archery bear opens August 15 across the entire bear hunt area. The season runs through December 27 or closes early if the statewide harvest hits 1,700 bears (last year's take was around 1,180, so early closure is unlikely). You can hold two tags this year but take only one bear per day, and it is non-lead, no bait, no dogs, with validation and reporting mandatory.
- August 15: B-zone archery opens. Most B zones (B1, B2, B3, B5, B6) run archery August 15 to September 6. B-4 opened earlier, July 25, and closes August 16. Confirm your exact B subzone dates in the Big Game Digest before you commit.
- Looking ahead, September 1: dove opener, first split September 1 to 15. The scouting you do this month is the limit you fill in September.
- Non-lead, every hunt, no exceptions. Certified non-lead ammunition is required for all hunting with a firearm anywhere in California. The right bullet weights thin out on the shelf as every opener approaches, so buy your rifle boxes now while you can still pick your load.

## From Field to Table: Turn the Freezer Into Field Food (Venison Jerky)

Here is a two-birds move for opener week. You are about to spend long, hot days glassing ridges, which means you need food you can stuff in a pack and forget about. And you have probably still got a lean roast or two from last year taking up freezer space you are about to need. Solve both at once: turn those old hindquarter roasts into jerky. Lean venison is the ideal jerky meat, because there is almost no fat to go rancid, and a batch made this week rides in your pack all season.

You will need:

- 2 lbs lean venison roast (hindquarter or round), every scrap of fat and silver skin trimmed off
- 1/2 cup soy sauce
- 1/4 cup Worcestershire sauce
- 2 tbsp brown sugar or honey
- 1 tbsp coarse black pepper
- 1 tsp garlic powder
- 1 tsp onion powder
- 1 tsp smoked paprika
- Optional heat: 1 tsp red pepper flakes or a good shot of hot sauce

The method:

1. Trim it hard. Fat is what turns jerky rancid, so cut away every bit of it and any silver skin. Firm the roast in the freezer for an hour or two so it slices clean, then cut strips about an eighth to a quarter inch thick. Slice with the grain for a chewy classic jerky, against the grain for a more tender bite.
1. Whisk the marinade together, drop the strips in, and refrigerate 6 to 24 hours. Longer means more flavor and more salt.
1. Pat the strips dry and lay them out so none are touching, on dehydrator trays or on oven racks set over a foil-lined sheet to catch drips.
1. Run a dehydrator at 160 degrees, or an oven at its lowest setting with the door cracked, for 4 to 8 hours. It is done when a strip bends and cracks but does not snap clean in half.
1. The safety step you do not skip with wild game: the USDA recommends jerky reach an internal 160 degrees to kill any pathogens. The easy path is to dehydrate at 160 the whole time, or to finish the dried strips in a 275-degree oven for 10 minutes. Do not shortcut this one.
1. Cool completely, then store airtight. It keeps for weeks in the fridge and months in the freezer. Portion a bag into your pack now so it is there on opening morning.

## Gear Check: Skin It Solo at the Truck

![](/media/8a38e2a7-4cbb-46cb-9cd4-799acb93b3fe.png)

HME Truck Hitch Game Hoist, Complete Kit

Once a buck is down and you can get a vehicle to it, the race is getting it hung, skinned, and cooling. This hoist drops into a standard 2-inch receiver on a truck, SUV, or UTV, so you do not need a tree. The kit includes a hand-crank winch, a steel gambrel, and a 360-degree swiveling shaft with a locking pin, so one person can crank a deer up, lock it, and spin it to work every side. It is rated to 400 pounds, telescopes from 74 to 102 inches, and rides on an adjustable support foot for stability on uneven ground.

It runs about $170 at Sportsman's Warehouse (check price and stock, it moves around). Pair it with the replaceable-blade knife (Issue 4) and your game bags (Issue 3): hoist, skin to shed body heat, then bag the quarters and get them on ice.

## The Showcase

![](/media/cec351c3-46c1-4993-ae28-9afc06bd97ef.png)

This week's Showcase caught the calendar turning. Connie A. of Durham sent in a clip of a young buck working the velvet off his new rack, raking it through the brush the way they do when it is ready to come off. It is one of the surest signs the season is closing in: the velvet peels, the antlers harden, and by the opener every buck on your cameras looks like a different animal. If you have been running summer cameras, you are watching the same thing play out right now.

That is exactly what we built The Showcase for, and it runs on you. Exclusive to subscribers only, so the people on this list are the only ones who see it. Grip-and-grins, a limit strap in the fog, the dog mid-retrieve, a kid's first bird, a trail-cam giant you are chasing this fall. Photo or video, if it is from your season, we want it. Every pick earns a permanent spot on our subscribers-only Showcase page at norcalhunt.com/showcase.

To get in: hit reply with your photo, and a sentence about it, and tell us how you want to be credited (we run first name, last initial, and town). The best one each week runs up top, and at the end of every month subscribers vote for a Showcase winner. Send us one to keep it rolling.

## Dog of the Week

![](/media/5277e0f9-e8fb-46dd-b384-59027d4706c5.png)

Meet "Ranger" and "Ford" Owner: Erick S.

Ranger (left, 8 years old) and Ford (right, 3 years old) are a two-dog team, pictured here backing up a late-season single-man limit. When these two are not working the blind, you will find them lounging around the house or logging as many summer days as they can up at Lake Almanor.

Missed a week? Catch up on every dog we have featured on our past Dogs of the Week page at norcalhunt.com/dogoftheweek.

## From the Field: More Than a Limit

"It took longer to set out the decoys than it did to shoot our limits."

Seven old college buddies, a cold north wind across the Sacramento Valley rice, and a steel-gray sky made for geese. What started as a rare reunion turned into one of those mornings you remember for years: specks, snows, and honkers finishing over the spread wave after wave until every hunter had filled on both dark and light geese. But as contributor Chad M. found on the long drive home, the limit was not the part that stuck with him.

Read the full story on norcalhunt.com/fieldstories

Got a hunt that turned into a story? A first buck, a close call, a comedy of errors, a last hunt with an old dog? Hit reply and tell us. The best ones run right here.

This briefing gets sharper when we hear from you. Drop us a quick reply and tell us:

1. What zones do you hunt most?
1. What are you chasing this fall: blacktail, ducks, doves, pigs, bear?

Last week's poll is in. We asked for your go-to backstrap prep, and bacon-wrapped medallions took the top spot. Cast-iron seared and sliced pink, grilled whole over coals, and chicken-fried with gravy all pulled votes, but the bacon-and-toothpick crowd carried the day. If you have not tried it, consider this your inspiration to cook what your fellow NorCal hunters are swearing by: wrap a backstrap medallion in bacon, pin it with a toothpick, and grill it over medium heat until the bacon crisps and the meat is still pink in the middle.

NorCal is dry and the fire picture is active heading into the opener. The biggest one in our backyard right now is the Biscar Fire in Lassen County. The Biscar Fire reached 69,352 acres and was 97% contained by late July. It is essentially fully suppressed with all evacuation orders lifted. CAL FIRE keeps fire potential at normal to above normal through September.

Before you load the truck:

- Confirm restrictions for your exact unit. Forest Service, BLM, and CAL FIRE rules change fast and vary by district, so check your specific ground before you go.

issues.blurb: Introducing The Showcase, our new subscribers-only photo feature. Plus a backstrap recipe worthy of a fresh blacktail, a value glass pick, the 2026 duck survey, and a black Lab named Gunner.
issues.body:
## Sunday, July 26, 2026

Welcome back. A week into the A-zone archery season, the first blacktail of 2026 are on the ground, and the calendar is about to get busy. Bow season is down to its final weekend, the rifle opener is two Saturdays away, and bear archery lands right behind it. This week we're cooking the best cut on the animal the way it deserves: a fresh blacktail backstrap, seared pink in cast iron. We've also got a value glass pick to get you seeing deer before the opener, a straight read on the 2026 duck survey and what it actually means for your season, and a fire picture that has gotten serious. And we're kicking off something new this week, The Showcase, our reader-photo feature. Let's get into it.

## The Board: Crucial Dates & Deadlines

- A-zone archery is in its final week. It closes Sunday, August 2. After this weekend, the bow window shuts. If you're still carrying a coastal blacktail tag, August 1 and 2 are your last two days. Confirm your subzone dates and either-sex rules in the 2026 Big Game Digest before you go, and remember you cannot take a deer with a firearm during archery season.
- B-4 archery is now OPEN (July 25 to August 16). B-4 is the early bird of the B zones. B-zone tags are valid in any B zone during either season, so if you drew or bought a B tag and want to hunt now, B-4 is your ticket. Everybody else in the B zones waits until August 15 (see below).
- Leftover ("restricted") deer tags go live August 2. If you struck out on a premium tag or want a second tag, unclaimed premium tags roll into the restricted pool. Starting the first business day after August 1, you can use a second deer tag to pick up a restricted or unrestricted tag over the counter or online, subject to availability. Some good tags quietly show up here. Log into your CDFW sales profile and check the current available-tag list.
- Saturday, August 8: Zone A general (rifle) opener. This is the big one, and it's two weekends out. A-zone general runs August 8 to September 20, one of the longest general seasons in the state. One buck per tag. If you're switching from bow to rifle, this is the week to group your certified non-lead load and get zeroed with the exact ammo you'll hunt. Non-lead can thin out on the shelf close to any opener, so don't wait on it.
- August 15: B-zone archery AND archery bear both open. Most of the B zones (B1, B2, B3, B5, B6) run archery August 15 to September 6. Archery bear opens the same day across the entire bear hunt area, also through September 6. More bear notes below.
- Looking ahead: September 1, dove opener (first split, September 1 to 15). We'll go deep on doves as it gets closer.

## From Field to Table: Cast-Iron Blacktail Backstrap, Seared Pink

If you punched a tag this month, the backstrap is your reward, and it's the one cut you do not want to overthink. This is the long loin that runs down either side of the spine: the one that turns venison skeptics into believers when you cook it right. It comes together fast, and the single rule is the same one we preached with wild duck back in Issue #3: pull it pink.

Wild venison is lean, with almost none of the marbling that carries a beef steak through an overcook. Take a backstrap past medium and it goes gray, dry, and livery, and all that careful field care from the last two issues dies right there on the cutting board. Cook it to a warm pink center and it's as good as anything you'll eat all year.

This scales to whatever you've got, one steak or a whole loin. There are no measurements here on purpose. Backstrap doesn't need a recipe card, it needs heat, fat, and restraint.

What you need: backstrap with the silverskin trimmed off, salt and pepper, a neutral oil that can take high heat, a good knob of butter, a few smashed garlic cloves, and a sprig or two of thyme or rosemary. That's it.

The method:

1. Pull the meat out ahead of time so it takes the chill off, and pat it bone dry. Cold, wet meat steams instead of searing. Season it hard all over with salt and pepper.
1. Get a cast-iron pan ripping hot with the oil, right to the edge of smoking. Lay the backstrap in and leave it alone. Sear until each side builds a deep brown crust, rolling a round loin to hit every face. Cut steaks get a quick hard sear; a whole loin takes a little longer.
1. Drop the heat, add the butter, garlic, and herbs, and once the butter foams, tilt the pan and spoon it over the meat again and again. This baste is where the flavor lives.
1. Cook to medium-rare and stop there. This is the whole game. Venison is lean, and a warm pink center is the difference between the best bite of the year and gray, livery disappointment. An instant-read thermometer takes out the guesswork, but the finger test or a small cut to peek works too. Remember it climbs a little more while it rests, so pull it a touch early.
1. Rest it before you cut. Non-negotiable. Slice in too soon and the juice you fought to keep runs out onto the board instead of staying in the meat.
1. Slice against the grain, spoon the pan butter over the top, and if you want a sauce, deglaze the hot pan with a splash of stock or red wine and let it reduce.

The one rule, again: medium-rare, then rest. A backstrap is too good a cut to gray out. Hand the skeptics at your table a pink, rested slice and watch them circle back for the end pieces. Then finish the rest of the animal the way we talked about last week, under vacuum and into the freezer, so a July blacktail eats like a gift in December.

## Gear Check: Glass Up for the Opener (It's Vortex Month)

![](/media/a6d3fd25-b288-4ec3-a7e6-570731802bae.png)

You don't walk up on coastal blacktail, you find them, and you find them by glassing the thick edges in the first and last hour of light. With the rifle opener two weeks out, good glass is the upgrade that puts the most deer in front of you.

Our value pick is Vortex across the board. Honest glass in low light, a tough build, and the unlimited lifetime VIP warranty behind all of it: damage it however you manage, they fix or replace it, no receipt needed. A 10x42 binocular is the do-everything choice for Northern California (drop to 8x42 for tight cover or shaky hands), a spotting scope earns its keep picking apart far hillsides, and if you're moving to the rifle, a solid Vortex scope covers you there too.

And the timing's right: July is Vortex Month at Sportsman's Warehouse, the year's best deals on Vortex glass, online and in store, often with a gift-card offer on select buys. If you've been meaning to upgrade or replace binoculars, a spotting scope, or a rifle scope before the season ramps up, this is the window. Check the current terms, it's a July-only thing.

## Waterfowl News: The 2026 Duck Survey Is Out. Here's What It Means For Your Fall.

Duck season feels a long way off in this heat, but the report that shapes it just landed. The U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service has released the field reports from the 2026 Waterfowl Breeding Population and Habitat Survey, the seven-decade-running count that flies transects across the northern breeding grounds every spring.

The short version: mixed, leaning dry. Crews found spring delays and drought across several key western breeding areas, which is not what you want to hear. There were bright spots too, including improved conditions in parts of the Dakotas and some recovery in the central Canadian boreal, but those may not fully offset the drier country elsewhere.

What that actually means for you, in plain terms. The young birds hatched on those breeding grounds this spring are the ducks that come down the Pacific Flyway this coming season. Dry breeding country generally means fewer juveniles in the fall flight, though the bright spots temper it. So this is a real, if early, signal about the flight headed our way.

The nuance a reliable newsletter owes you: the hard population numbers, the formal Waterfowl Population Status report, come out later this year, and those numbers set the framework for the 2027-2028 season, not this one. This coming season's NorCal dates and limits are already locked, and we covered them back in Issue #3: Balance of State ducks and geese October 24 to January 31, specklebelly cut to 6 a day, ducks at 7 with the usual sub-limits.

And the local wildcard that matters more than any continental number: water in the Sacramento Valley rice. ## Sunday, July 19, 2026

Welcome back. A week into the archery opener, the first blacktail of 2026 are hitting the ground, and if you connected, the work is only half done. This week we're covering the part nobody talks about: how to keep your meat cold on a hot drive home, and the freezer tool that saves more venison than any knife. We've also got the dates that matter as the rifle opener and bear season close in, a black Lab pup you'll want to meet, and a father-daughter story out of the Tehama fog that'll stick with you. Round it out with a straight read on the fire picture and a quick poll at the very bottom on our new weather page, and you're set. Let's get into it.

## The Board: Crucial Dates & Deadlines

- July 15 is behind us. The elk, antelope, and bighorn tag payment window closed Tuesday. If you drew and paid, you're locked in for the season ahead.
- Zone A archery is OPEN through August 2. You've got two weekends left in the coastal blacktail archery season. Warm mornings, thick cover, deer moving in the first and last hour of light. Confirm your subzone dates and either-sex rules in the 2026 Big Game Digest before you head out.
- Zone A general (rifle) opens Saturday, August 8 (runs Aug 8 to September 20, one of the longest general seasons in the state). Just three weeks out. One buck per tag. If you're switching from archery to rifle, this is the week to pattern your non-lead loads and get zeroed. Certified non-lead can thin out on the shelf close to any opener, so don't wait.
- No tag yet? A-zone is still on the table. A-zone tags are unrestricted and available over the counter, no draw required, so there's still time to put together a last-minute blacktail hunt. Grab one online or from a license agent (make sure your 2026-27 license is current first) and you can be in the field this season.
- B-zone archery opens August 15, with one early exception. Most of the B zones (B1, B2, B3, B5, and B6) run archery August 15 to September 6, with the general season following September 19. The outlier is B-4, which opens earliest of the bunch: archery July 25 to August 16. B-zone tags are valid in any B zone during either season, but confirm your exact subzone dates in the 2026 Big Game Digest before you commit.
- Leftover premium deer tags: August 2. Unclaimed premium tags go on sale starting August 2. If you struck out in the main draw, it's a second shot at a good tag.
- Looking ahead: September 1, dove opener (first split, Sept 1 to 15). More on doves as it gets closer.

## From Field to Table: The Drive Home Is Where Good Meat Dies

Back in Issue #6 we covered field-dressing a blacktail against the clock. Here's the part nobody talks about: you can do everything right on the mountain and still hand your buck to the bacteria on the drive home. A cooler baking in a truck bed on I-5 in July is an oven with a lid. The cooler game is won before you ever pull the trigger, and it comes down to three words: cold, dry, airflow.

Start cold. Ice the cooler down the night before so it's already frigid when the meat goes in, or at least throw a bag of ice in for the drive out to pre-chill it. A warm cooler steals your cold before it ever touches the meat. Block ice and frozen water jugs last far longer than cubes, so run a mix: cubes to chill fast, blocks and jugs to hold. Frozen jugs are the sleeper pick because they keep your meat dry as they thaw, and you can refreeze them for the next trip.

Keep the meat up out of the water. This is the one that gets people. Meat sitting in a pool of meltwater goes waterlogged, gray, and sour, and it happens fast. Bag your quarters in breathable game bags first, then set them on a rack, a grate, or even a couple of frozen jugs so they ride above the melt. Crack the drain plug and tilt the cooler slightly so the water runs out while the meat stays dry and cold.

Bring at least as much ice as meat. A one-to-one ice-to-meat ratio is the floor in July heat, more if you can swing it. Pack it snug, because a full cooler holds cold far better than a half-empty one. On a long haul, plan an ice run partway: a gas-station bag of ice on top of your bagged quarters can save a whole cooler.

Keep it out of the sun. A cooler riding in a black truck bed in direct sun is losing the fight no matter how much ice you loaded. Ride it in the cab if you can, or throw a light-colored blanket or tarp over it and park in the shade at every stop. And quit opening it. Every peek dumps your cold air, so if you want drinks for the road, bring a second cheap cooler and leave the meat cooler shut.

Then close it out at home. Don't let the cooler become long-term storage in a hot garage. The second you're back, move the meat to the fridge, the cutting table, or the freezer. Cold, dry, and handled quickly the whole way from the mountain to the freezer is the entire ballgame, and it does more for how your venison tastes this winter than any marinade ever will.

## Gear Check: Vacuum Sealer (Weston Pro-2300)

![](/media/e80b3876-6c86-46f6-8d1e-108137a91937.png)

All that careful meat care in the field and on the drive home comes down to one last step: how you put it away. And this is where a lot of good venison quietly dies. Butcher paper and freezer bags trap air, and trapped air is freezer burn, the dry, gray, cardboard-flavored fate of too many backstraps by February. A vacuum sealer is the cheapest insurance you can buy on a whole season of meat.

The value play is a solid external sealer. The Weston Pro line and the FoodSaver GameSaver models pull the air out of the bag and heat-seal it shut, and a properly sealed cut holds its quality several times longer than paper or zip bags, often two to three years deep in the freezer. Look for a moist setting or manual pulse control (fresh venison is wet), a built-in bag cutter and roll storage so you can size bags to the cut, and enough duty cycle that it won't overheat halfway through a deer. The honest limits: external sealers can fight you on bloody, wet meat, and they need a cool-down between long runs.

One field tip: package your ground meat in flat one-pound bricks. They freeze fast, stack like books, and thaw quick.

## Bear on Deck

If you're carrying a bear tag into blacktail country this fall, know your dates:

- Archery bear runs August 15 to September 6 across the entire bear hunt area.
- General bear opens right alongside the general deer opener in zones A, B, C, D, and X8, X9A, X9B, X10, and X12, and runs through December 27. In A-zone, that means bear comes in with the rifle opener on August 8.
- The whole season (archery and general combined) closes early the moment the statewide harvest hits 1,700 bears. Check the CDFW bear harvest tracking page before you head out.
- Under the current framework you can hold up to two bear tags in a license year, though the possession limit is still two and you can take only one bear per day. No bait, no dogs, and non-lead ammo, same as everything else in California.

Late summer, bears are hammering acorns, berries, and green. Glass the same first-and-last light you're already hunting for deer, and you may fill two tags on one trip.

## Dog of the Week

![](/media/ae0a50a1-ba06-4377-bbc5-373310155fca.png)

Meet "Rhett" Owner: Rowan T, Chico, CA

Rhett is a 12-week-old black Lab and future duck dog with an obsession for water and a relentless drive to retrieve. He's projected to top out around 80 pounds, but for now he's burning that endless puppy energy chewing on anything he can reach. It won't be long before he swaps those chew toys for retrieves in the duck blind.

## From the Field: Lessons in the Clouds

"You'll catch up on school," he said, loading the truck before dawn. "There are things you can only learn out here."

The week Paige A's dad pulled her out of class for the late-season G1 hunt in Tehama County, she figured missing school was the big deal. He knew better. What followed was a Week of Low clouds draped over the ridges, mist dripping off the pines, and a still-hunt along a timbered ridge in the kind of wet weather that keeps most people home and gets blacktail on their feet. When a three-point stepped broadside out of the drifting fog, Paige was carrying Pop's worn lever-action .308, her dad beside her with the only three words that mattered: take your time. It's a story about patience, foul-weather blacktail, and three generations meeting in one spot on a Tehama mountain.

Quick one worth knowing while you're sweating through July: those green rice checks you're driving past in the Sacramento Valley right now are this winter's duck hunting. Summer's planted, flooded rice becomes the surrogate wetland that carries millions of Pacific Flyway ducks and geese through the season, roughly 300,000 acres of it flooded each winter, and it provides the bulk of the food those birds live on. A strong crop in the field today is a strong Balance of State season in December. Two sides of the same coin.

No sugarcoating it: NorCal is hot and the fire picture is serious. The state is at Preparedness Level 5 (the highest there is), fires are already burning in our backyard (the Elephant Fire in Sierra County plus multiple Lassen County starts), and Red Flag Warnings keep hitting the far northeast with critically dry fuels. Before you load the truck:

issues.body:
## Sunday, July 12, 2026

Welcome back. The wait is officially over — Zone A archery opened yesterday, which means the first blacktail of the 2026 season are already on their way to the freezer. If you punched a tag this weekend, congratulations, and read the Field to Table section below closely: a July deer is a race against the heat the second it hits the ground.

And if you drew a premium tag but haven't paid for it yet, stop scrolling. Tuesday is the day that costs people their once-in-a-lifetime hunt every single year.

## The Board: Crucial Dates & Deadlines

- July 15, 5:00 p.m. PDT — Elk, Antelope & Bighorn Tag Payment. FINAL 72 HOURS. This is the one that bites hunters every year, and we've flagged it three issues running for a reason. If you drew a premium elk, pronghorn antelope, or bighorn sheep tag, successful applicants were notified in early July and payment is due by 5:00 p.m. PDT this Tuesday, July 15. Miss the window and your tag rolls to an alternate — no exceptions, no mercy, no "I was busy at work." Log into your CDFW online sales profile today, confirm your status, and pay it now.
- Premium deer drew? You may still owe a tag fee. If you drew a premium deer tag (like an X-zone), don't assume you're clear because you paid an application fee up front. Confirm in your CDFW account whether a tag fee is still due by the July 15 deadline to claim it.
- Zone A Archery Is OPEN (July 11 – August 2). Coastal blacktail, thick cover, warm mornings, one of the earliest deer hunts in the country. If you're heading out this week, confirm your exact subzone dates, boundaries, and antler/either-sex rules in the 2026 Big Game Digest before you go — A-zone splits into units and you want to be standing on the right line. Reminder: you cannot use a firearm to take a deer during archery season.
- Looking ahead: August 8 — Zone A general (rifle) opener (runs Aug 8 – Sep 20). September 1 — Dove opener (first split, Sept 1–15).
- Still on last year's license? The 2026–27 license year began July 1; last year's license and validations expired June 30. Everything from here — the archery opener, summer hogs, dove validations — requires the new license.

## Last Week's Poll: The Freezer Confession

We asked you to be honest last week: how much venison is currently sitting in your freezer right now? You answered, and it came down to a dead-even split:

- 50% — "Cleaned out, ready for August."
- 50% — "A couple of backstrap steaks and some ground."
- 0% — "It's a logistical nightmare."

So either this is the most disciplined, freezer-organized readership in Northern California... or nobody's willing to admit they've still got last season's deer buried under a bag of tri-tip and a forgotten sack of dove breasts.

Either way, the timing lines up: freezers are empty or close to it, a fresh blacktail season just opened, and the field-dressing playbook below is how you fill them back up clean. Thanks to everyone who voted on our first-ever confession poll — we'll keep them coming.

## From Field to Table: Field Dressing a Blacktail in the Heat

Back in Issue #1 we talked about cooling a hog down fast in 90-degree foothills. Now it's deer's turn — and a July blacktail is the same problem with a nicer backstrap. The single biggest factor in how your venison tastes this fall isn't your recipe. It's what you do in the first 30 minutes after the animal is down. Get the guts out, get the heat out, and get it clean. Here's the whole job, start to finish.

Before you touch a blade: tag it. California requires you to fill out and attach your tag to the carcass immediately upon harvest, before you move or process the animal. Do it first. Snap your photos fast, then get to work — the clock is already running.

What you want on your belt: a sharp knife (a replaceable-blade knife — our Issue #4 Gear Check — is made for exactly this hot, fast work), nitrile gloves, a couple of game bags, a zip tie or short length of cord, and water. A small bone saw is a bonus, not a requirement.

The traditional field-dress, step by step:

1. Position the deer on its back with the head slightly uphill so fluids drain away from the chest cavity, not into it. Brace it with your knees or wedge it against rocks or brush.
1. Ring the bung. Cut a circle around the anus (and around the vulva on a doe), work it free, and tie it off with a zip tie so nothing leaks back into the meat as you work. A "butt-out" tool makes this a ten-second job.
1. Open the hide only. Pinch the skin at the base of the ribcage and make a shallow starter cut. Slide two fingers into the opening in a "V," lift the abdominal wall up and away from the guts, and run your blade between your fingers down to the pelvis — blade facing up, riding on your fingers. This is the whole game: a nicked stomach or intestine spills gut content into the cavity and taints meat fast. Go slow here so you can go fast everywhere else.
1. Free the diaphragm. Roll the deer onto its side. Reach up into the chest and cut the diaphragm — the sheet of muscle separating the guts from the lungs — away from the rib cage all the way around.
1. Cut high and pull. Reach as far up into the chest as you can, grab the windpipe and esophagus, and cut them off high. Then pull down and back — the entire gut package and the heart and lungs should roll out together onto the ground.
1. Save the good stuff. Want the heart and liver? Bag them now and get them on ice — organs spoil faster than muscle.
1. Clean, don't drown. Wipe the cavity out with a clean cloth or paper towels. Resist the urge to dump creek water in it unless you can dry it back out — standing moisture is what bacteria wants. Dry is better than wet.
1. Prop it open and get it to shade. Wedge a stick across the chest cavity to keep air moving through it, and get the carcass out of the sun immediately.

Then the heat game (same rules as the hog): skin it to shed body heat, quarter it if you're packing out, use breathable game bags instead of plastic, and if it's going in a cooler, keep the meat elevated off the pooling melt water. Cool, clean, home.

Know the gutless method too. In steep coastal blacktail country where you're packing quarters out on your back, a lot of experienced hunters skip gutting entirely — they skin one side, take the two quarters, the backstrap, and the tenderloin, roll the deer, and repeat, never opening the abdominal cavity at all. It's faster, cleaner, and there's zero risk of tainting meat on a hot gut pile. Worth learning before you need it.

## Gear Check: See in the Dark, Work in the Dark

![](/media/1e2f4a65-7b80-42a4-a138-40947b4641db.png)

Rechargeable Headlamp with Red-Light Mode (Black Diamond Spot 400)

The game move in the thin light at the very edges of the day — the first hour and the last. That means you're hiking in before legal light and, if you connect on an evening deer, field dressing it after dark. A phone flashlight in your teeth doesn't cut it when both hands are inside a rib cage.

A good headlamp fixes two problems at once. Get one with a red-light mode — red preserves your night vision on the walk in and spooks game far less than a white beam — plus enough white output (around 300–400 lumens) to light up a blood trail or a dressing job. Look for USB-rechargeable with a battery you can actually top off from your truck, a comfortable band that stays put when you look down, and a housing that shrugs off rain and sweat.

It typically streets around $40–$50 (check current pricing). For the price of a box of shells, it's the difference between confidently working a carcass at 9 p.m. and rushing a job you can't see — right when careful, clean work matters most for your meat.

## From the Field: Deer Sledding with Pops

"I knew I wasn't going to make it if I dragged him," Dad would say with a grin.

Some of our absolute favorite hunting memories have nothing to do with filling a tag. They happen after dark, when the rifles are cased, the coffee pot is hissing over the coals, and the October chill settles into the pines above Susanville.

Growing up, I had one legendary story I made my dad tell me every single night at camp. It involved a snowy ridge, fading daylight, and my dad riding a harvested buck down the mountain like a kid on a toboggan—using the antlers as handlebars.

Read the full story on norcalhunt.com →

Got a hunt that turned into a story? A close call, a comedy of errors, a first deer, a last hunt with an old dog? Hit reply and tell us — the best ones run right here.

## Dog of the Week

![](/media/85821bab-87c5-455a-95d4-1cbad02d0f64.png)

Meet "Mae" — Owner: Mike and Betsy K., Orland, CA.

Mae is officially our first "occasional good mutt" to grace the briefing, proving you don't need a fancy pedigree to get your hunt on. She has found her one true calling: flushing gophers during irrigation season. Working alongside her partner-in-crime, Apollo, she keeps the local pest population firmly in check. She might not be good for much else—but as her owner freely admits, at least she's kind of cute.

Want your dog featured? Hit reply, send us a clean photo of your hunting partner, and give us a quick 2–3 sentence blurb on what they hunt and where they earn their kibble. Pointers, flushers, retrievers, and the occasional very good mutt all qualify.

## Regulation Reminders

- Headed to the Sierra? Know the CWD zones. Chronic wasting disease was first confirmed in California deer in 2024, and CDFW now runs four CWD Management Zones with mandatory sampling of hunter-harvested deer — D7, X9a, X9b, and X9c. If you're hunting those units, you must submit your deer for testing, and carcass-movement restrictions may apply. Coastal A-zone hunters are outside the zones, but if your fall plans include the central or eastern Sierra, check the current rules and testing sites at wildlife.ca.gov/CWD before you hunt.
- Report your tag. Deer tag reporting is due by the regulatory deadline whether you fill it or not — skipping it means a non-reporting penalty on your next purchase.

## Community: Help Us Build the Pack

This briefing gets sharper when we hear from you. Drop us a quick reply and tell us:

1. What zones do you hunt most?
1. What are you chasing this fall — blacktail, ducks, doves, pigs?
1. How can we make the weekly briefing better?

Got a hunting partner who lives in the foothills, the rice, or along the riverbanks? Forward this briefing and point them to norcalhunt.com. Word of mouth from real hunters is how we grow.

## Conditions: Heat & Fire — Read This Before You Head Out

NorCal summer is in full swing. A severe heat wave is baking the state — triple digits in the valleys, critically low humidity — and after a winter that delivered a below average snowpack, fuels are cured early and fire activity is running ahead of pace. Red Flag Warnings have been landing across parts of the region, including the far northeast (Surprise Valley and eastern Lassen).

Before you load the truck: confirm current fire restrictions for your exact unit (Forest, BLM, and CAL FIRE rules change fast) and don't be the ignition near dry grass. And beat the heat — hunt the first and last hour around water and shade, carry more water than you think you need, and remember a deer down at midday needs to be dressed and cooling immediately.

Stay safe out there, get your gear cleaned, and we'll see you in the field.

— The NorCal Hunt Team

- Still on last year's license? The 2026–27 license year began July 1; last year's license and validations expired June 30. Anything you do from here — the archery opener, summer hogs, buying dove validations — requires the new license. While you're in the cart, grab your Upland Game Bird Validation and knock out free HIP registration now so you're not scrambling the night before dove opener.
- Looking ahead: August 8 — A-zone general (rifle) opener. September 1 — dove opener (first split). More on doves below.

## From Field to Table: Clear-the-Freezer Dove Poppers

Dove opener is six weeks out, and if you had a good first split last September you've probably still got a bag or two of dove breasts buried in the back of the freezer. Clear them out now — there's no sense stacking fresh birds on top of last year's. And there's no better way to send off a pile of dove than the recipe that's practically the official dish of opening weekend: bacon-wrapped jalapeño poppers. They're forgiving, they disappear off the plate, and they turn a lean little breast into the best reason to fire up the grill.

You'll need (makes about 24 poppers):

- 24 dove breast halves (roughly 12 birds), boned out
- 12 slices thin-cut bacon, each cut in half
- 4 oz cream cheese, softened
- 3–4 fresh jalapeños, seeded and sliced into strips (leave some membrane in if you want more heat)
- Kosher salt, black pepper, garlic powder
- Optional marinade: Italian dressing, or a quick mix of soy sauce and Worcestershire
- Optional glaze: a drizzle of hot honey or your favorite BBQ sauce
- Toothpicks

The method:

1. If you've got the time, marinate the dove breasts a few hours in Italian dressing or the soy-Worcestershire mix — it seasons and tenderizes lean birds that have been in the freezer a while. Pat them dry before you build.
1. Season the breasts with salt, pepper, and garlic powder.
1. Build each popper: lay a dab of cream cheese and a strip of jalapeño against a breast, then wrap the whole thing in a half-slice of bacon and pin it with a toothpick.
1. Grill over medium, indirect heat, turning every few minutes, until the bacon is crisp and rendered and the breast is just cooked through — roughly 15–20 minutes. Keep a cooler zone open, because bacon grease will flare up.
1. If you're glazing, brush on the hot honey or BBQ sauce in the last 2–3 minutes so it sets without burning.
1. Rest a couple of minutes, pull the toothpicks, and serve hot.

Doneness note: Dove is lean and unforgiving — the second you blow past done it turns liver-y and tough, so pull the poppers as soon as the bacon crisps and the breast is cooked through. One more heads-up for the table: dove often carries a stray shot pellet or two, so remind your guests to eat with that in mind.

## Gear Check: See the Yardage Before You Draw

![](/media/b174081f-790e-4506-a359-7cb42fa1cbce.png)

Laser Rangefinder (Vortex Diamondback HD 2000)

Bowhunting coastal blacktail means steep ground, tight cover, and shots where guessing "forty-ish" turns a clean hole into a wounded deer. A rangefinder erases the guesswork — and for archery, the feature that matters most isn't max distance, it's angle compensation. Shoot up or down a ridge and the true horizontal distance your arrow needs to fly is shorter than the line-of-sight number; a rangefinder with angle-comp gives you the actual "shoot-to" yardage so you hold dead-on.

The Diamondback HD 2000 is the value play here. It reads far past any ethical shot you'd ever take with a bow or a rifle, the glass is clean enough to range in low light at the edges of the day when blacktail actually move, and it's backed by Vortex's unlimited lifetime VIP warranty — if it ever quits on you, they fix or replace it, no receipt required. It typically streets around $250–300 (check current pricing and specs before you buy). If you're stretching to rifle range in August too, angle-comp plus honest glass covers both seasons in one tool.

## Upland News: Dove Opener Is Six Weeks Out — Prep Now

It's the unofficial kickoff to California's hunting calendar, and it sneaks up fast. The first dove split runs September 1 through 15 statewide, with a second split in November. The daily bag is 15 mourning and white-winged doves combined, no more than 10 of which may be white-winged, and possession is triple the daily.

Two things worth handling now, not on August 30:

- Validations and shells. You'll need a valid hunting license, the Upland Game Bird Validation, and your free HIP number to hunt doves. Nonlead shot is required for taking dove — and any game with a firearm — anywhere in California. The small upland shot sizes vanish from shelves by late August every year, so buy your nonlead boxes early.
- Start glassing. Evenings on water sources and cut grain fields will show you where birds are trading. The scouting you do in July is the limit you fill in September.

Meet "Shadow" — Owner: Tad A., Durham, CA

At 8 years old, this seasoned Springer Spaniel is an absolute mallard machine in the rice, proving year after year that heart and drive beat size every single day. He cuts through the heavy winter tule cover with ease and sits dead-quiet in the blind when the birds are working. When he's off the clock, Shadow likes to unwind with a dip in the backyard pool and stay sharp playing with his local crew—Chewy, Cali, and Tilly.

## Conditions: Heat & Fire — Read This Before the Opener

NorCal summer is here in full, and this one's running hot. Vegetation across the region has been drying out since mid-May and fire activity is ahead of pace. Red Flag Warnings — strong winds, low humidity, and dry fuels — have been recurring across Northern California, and fire restrictions are already landing on public land ahead of the holiday.

Before you load the truck for a scout or the opener:

- Check restrictions for your exact unit. National Forest, BLM, and CAL FIRE restrictions can change fast and vary by district. Confirm your specific ground before you go.
- Beat the heat. Game moves in the first and last hour of light — plan your archery sits around water and shaded bedding, and carry far more water than you think you need on a July ridge.
- Don't be the ignition. Avoid anything that throws a spark near dry vegetation, and have a plan in case conditions turn.

issues.body:
Welcome back to the briefing. The "anticipation phase" is officially over. Big game results are in your account, the new license year kicks off this week, and California's earliest deer season opens in under two weeks. If you've been coasting since the draw closed, this is your nudge — it's go time.

## The Board: Crucial Dates & Deadlines

- The Ultimate NorCal Calendar: Looking for the full picture? We built an easily navigable, one-stop shop for your hunting season, drawing deadline, and opener across the state. Bookmark [norcalhunt.com/seasondates] to stay a step ahead of the regulations all year long. Did we leave something out? Reply to this email with any additional information you would like to see on this page.
- July 1 — New License Year Begins. Your 2026–27 California hunting license is valid from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027. Last year's license expires June 30, so buy your new one before your first hunt of the season. While you're in the cart, grab the validations and stamps you'll actually use this fall — Upland Game Bird Validation, HIP registration.
